## Episode S2·E5 — The Convergence Theorems

#### The Measure of All Things, Season Two, Episode Five

### The Question, Restated

Good day, sir.

If the Lebesgue integral were a product — and I have occasionally marketed it as one — tonight is the feature list that justifies the migration. Everything before was installation.

The question first, restated with the full weight it has accumulated, for no question in this course has a longer file. When does the integral of a limit equal the limit of the integrals? It was flagged in the first season's first evening, among Fourier's casualties. It was opened as a formal account — the swap account — in Season One, Episode Four, at the scene of the rearrangement outrage, with instalments scheduled through the end of this season. Episode Seven of that season paid the first: limits moved past limits, under the uniform license, over the corpse of Cauchy's false theorem. The season finale paid the second: the limit moved past the integral, again under uniformity, over the corpse of the moving spike — and I filed, you may recall, a codicil with the payment: the uniform license is sufficient and brutally expensive; sufficient, not necessary; a license, not the law. I asked you to hold its stinginess in mind as the standard to be beaten. And I quote the account's own opening paper back to you, as promised the night it was signed: Season Two, I said then, has crown jewels — the theorems that license the swap — and I say this now so you may hold me to it. You held; tonight I pay. The stakes, in your trade's plain terms: every time a training loop swaps a limit with an expectation — every convergence proof for an estimator, every exchange of gradient and average, every passage to the limit under an integral of losses — the manoeuvre stands on tonight's theorems or it does not stand at all. Tonight, sir, the account is closed — the third and final instalment, the crown jewels of this season and arguably of the entire course: three theorems that move limits past integrals for a licensing fee so small that Season One would have refused to believe the invoice. Monotone convergence. Fatou's lemma. Dominated convergence. By the hour's end, each will be proved — strategy aloud, paper in full — the additivity credit issued last week will be discharged on schedule, and your trade's daily habit of swapping a limit and an expectation will hold, at last, a theorem instead of a hope.

---

### The Three Escapes

Before the licenses, the crimes — and here the season pays one of its most instructive dividends, because the new machinery does not merely prove the theorems; it explains, exhaustively, what could ever go wrong. Mass, sir, escapes in exactly three ways, and I shall show you each as a picture.

Escape the first: off to the horizon. The marching bump — a block of unit mass sitting on the interval from n to n plus one, marching rightward as n grows. At every fixed point, the bump eventually passes and is gone: the pointwise limit is zero everywhere. But every term carries mass one; the integrals hold at one while the limit integrates to nought. The mass was not destroyed; it emigrated — horizontally, to infinity, one step per term.

Escape the second: up the spike. Season One's finale specimen, returning for its final appearance: height n on ground one over n — the tent thinner and taller with every term, mass fixed at one, pointwise limit zero. The mass climbs, sir: vertical emigration, the ground shrinking under it until in the limit it stands on nothing.

Escape the third: spread thin. Height one over n on the ground from nought to n — mass one, spread ever wider and flatter. The limit is zero — indeed the convergence is uniform, the sag everywhere at most one over n — and yet each term's mass is one. The mass neither marched nor climbed; it diluted, across ground that grew as fast as the height fell.

Note the accounting common to all three: no term destroys mass — each carries its unit faithfully — and yet the limit is destitute. The mass is conserved along the sequence and absent from its destination; it escapes not from the functions but from every fixed observer's window, horizontally past any frame, vertically past any ceiling, or laterally past any width. Three pictures, sir: the bump, the spike, the spread. Horizontal escape, vertical escape, dilution. And the theorem-shaped fact of the evening is this: that is the complete list. There is no fourth escape. Every failure of the swap, however dressed, is one of these three in costume — and each of tonight's licenses is engineered to bar specific exits. Note, before we leave the gallery, what the spread proves about Season One's prize instrument: its convergence is uniform, and the swap fails anyway. On unbounded ground, even the expensive license does not suffice — the finale's interchange theorem leaned on the interval's finite width, quietly, and the spread is what happens when nothing does. Uniformity was never the true currency, sir. Domination is — and we shall now buy it properly.

---

### The Climbing License

The first theorem bars every exit at once, by the simplest possible means: it forbids descent.

The monotone convergence theorem. Let a sequence of nonnegative measurable functions climb — each term at least its predecessor, pointwise — toward a limit function. Then the integral of the limit is the limit of the integrals. No domination, no uniformity, no finiteness — the limit and the integrals may all be infinite, and the theorem holds regardless, the two sides infinite together or finite together and equal. Climbing mass cannot escape: the bump would have to abandon ground it holds — descent; the spike would have to lower its skirts — descent; the spread likewise. Monotonicity bars all three exits with one clause.

The proof strategy, aloud, in two halves. One half is free: each climbing term sits below the limit, so each integral sits below the limit's integral — monotonicity of the integral, last week's manners — and the climbing integrals, a monotone sequence of numbers, converge by Season One's oldest license to something at most the limit's integral. The substance is the other half: the climbing integrals reach every under-staircase of the limit. Here is the idea, and it is the season's signature move wearing evening dress. Fix an under-staircase of the limit and offer it a discount: choose a rate c, strictly below one, and ask only that the climbing sequence overtake the discounted staircase — c times the storeys, rather than the storeys entire. Where does the n-th term suffice? On some citizen set; and as n grows these sufficiency sets swell — the climb is monotone — toward everything: at any point, the limit strictly exceeds the discounted storey, so some term already does. Now the crankshaft turns — continuity of measure along swelling chains, proved in this season's first evening for exactly this moment: each storey's ground is exhausted from within, the simple integral follows its grounds, and the climbing integrals dominate c times the staircase's full price. Let the discount tend to full price; the climbing integrals dominate every under-staircase; hence the supremum itself — which is, by ring sixteen, the integral of the limit. The desk writes every epsilon; the ear retains: discount, swell, exhaust, and let the discount expire. Beppo Levi's theorem, the trade also calls it, nineteen oh six; the season's engine, first crankshaft dividend at full torque. The clauses travel with the usual amnesty — climbing almost everywhere toward a limit almost everywhere suffices, null exceptions patched at the desk — and the sign clause is load-bearing, not clerical: a climbing sequence of signed functions can start at minus infinity's doorstep and climb forever without its integrals following; the desk's descending-tower specimen, read upside down, is the two-line witness.

One application before the corollaries, sir, chosen because Season One's finale had to refuse it. Integrate one over the square root of x on the interval from nought to one — unbounded near the origin, no ticket for Riemann's machine proper, an improper integral by the old regime's grace. The new regime needs no grace: truncate at one over n — the truncations climb, each bounded and honest — the truncated integrals compute by the schoolroom rule to two minus two over the square root of n, climbing to two; and the monotone license passes the limit: the integral is two, exactly, as an honest Lebesgue integral, no impropriety about it. The absolutely convergent improper integrals of Season One are absorbed wholesale by this one manoeuvre — truncate, climb, license — and the desk retires the relevant half of last week's boundary post on precisely this argument.

---

### The Credit, Discharged

And the machine now completes itself, sir, on schedule — the one-week maturity, honoured to the day.

Last week I issued, plainly flagged, the construction's final credit: additivity of the integral — that the integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals — proved only on the bounded estate, stated on credit beyond it. Watch the discharge. Take two nonnegative measurable functions; take their dyadic staircases, climbing as the staircase theorem provides; the sums of the staircases climb toward the sum of the functions; simple functions add exactly — last week's storey bookkeeping; and the monotone convergence theorem passes the addition through the limit. The integral of the sum is the sum of the integrals, on all nonnegative measurable functions whatsoever, and thence — gains and losses, the usual split — on all integrable ones. Debt fourteen: discharged, first corollary of the first crown jewel, precisely as the register scheduled.

And a second corollary follows so fast it barely touches the ground, resolving a question this course has carried since the rearrangement outrage: series and integrals swap freely when the terms are nonnegative. A series of nonnegative measurable functions is a climbing sequence of partial sums; additivity prices each partial sum; the monotone theorem passes the limit: the integral of the sum of a nonnegative series is the sum of the integrals, always — divergence included, both sides infinite together. No conditions, sir, beyond the sign. The rearrangement theorem taught you that signed infinite arithmetic is treacherous; tonight's corollary is the other shore: nonnegative infinite arithmetic commutes with everything in the building. The trade calls the pair — swap freely when nonnegative; check absolutely then swap when signed — the standard operating procedure, and Episode Seven will canonize it for double integrals under Tonelli's and Fubini's names. It begins here.

---

### The One-Way Valve

The second jewel is an inequality, and I shall spend a moment making its direction unforgettable, because half its citations in the wild are citations of its direction alone.

Fatou's lemma. For any sequence of nonnegative measurable functions — no monotonicity, no domination, nothing but the sign — the integral of the limit inferior is at most the limit inferior of the integrals. In the vernacular, sir: mass can be lost in the limit, never created. The three escapes are all losses — the bump's mass leaves, the spike's mass leaves, the spread's mass leaves; in every case the limit holds less than the terms carried. Fatou says that is the only direction the books can err: whatever survives to the limit was always there, term by term, in the liminf's honest accounting. A one-way valve on mass.

The mnemonic, before the proof, since the direction is the lemma's soul: the integrals remember mass that the limit has forgotten. The spike's integrals remember the unit that climbed away; its limit knows nothing. So the integrals' liminf stands at or above the limit's integral — never below. If you misremember the direction, sir, the spike corrects you in five seconds; I recommend the spike.

The proof rides the first jewel in four sentences — narrated entire, since the desk needs barely more. The infima of the tails — the running worst cases — form a climbing sequence, climbing by construction toward the limit inferior. Each tail-infimum sits below its own term, so its integral sits below that term's integral, hence below the tail's worst integral. Monotone convergence passes the climb on the left; the right side's tail-infima are the limit inferior of the integrals by definition. Valve proved. And the spike certifies the inequality strict: limit zero, integrals one — mass genuinely lost, the valve genuinely one-way. The desk adds the standing caution with a two-line specimen: no mirror statement for limsup holds without further hypotheses, and the sign condition is not decorative.

---
### The Crown Jewel

And now the theorem the season was built to reach, sir — the one your trade runs on daily, the one whose absence Season One could only paper over with uniformity's premium.

The dominated convergence theorem. Let a sequence of measurable functions converge pointwise — almost everywhere suffices, the amnesty extending every clause tonight — to a limit. Suppose the sequence is dominated: a single integrable function, one lid, sits above every term's absolute value, every term, everywhere. Then the limit is integrable, the integrals converge to the limit's integral — and the swap is licensed.

Hear the license's economy against the escapes. The bump cannot march under a lid: an integrable lid over every translate would carry mass along the whole horizon — infinite mass, not integrable. The spike cannot climb: a lid over every spike majorizes one over x near the origin — infinite mass again. The spread cannot dilute: a lid over every spreading term covers a fixed plateau on every frame out to infinity — infinite once more; the desk computes all three in a line apiece. One hypothesis, sir — one integrable ceiling — and all three exits are bricked shut at once. That is what domination means: the mass has nowhere to go, because the lid is a fixed, finite roof over the entire procession, and mass that cannot move must converge. Compare the price against Season One's: uniformity demanded control of every discrepancy at every point simultaneously, and still needed finite ground; the lid asks one function, checked once, and covers infinite ground without comment. What those theorems ask, sir, is nearly nothing — and now you see what this season's machinery was too weak to buy until tonight.

The proof, and it is the evening's most elegant three minutes: the crown jewel is Fatou's valve, applied twice, once from each side. The lid plus each term is nonnegative — the lid absorbs the negative parts, that is its office; Fatou's valve on that sequence, after the additivity of the credit's discharge cancels the lid's finite integral from both sides — lawful, the lid being integrable — yields: the limit's integral is at most the liminf of the integrals. The lid minus each term is likewise nonnegative; the valve again, the lid cancelling again, and the inequality arrives reversed: the limsup of the integrals is at most the limit's integral. Liminf above, limsup below, both pinned to the same number: the integrals converge, to exactly the limit's integral. Two applications of a one-way valve, facing opposite directions, make a two-way license. The desk writes the cancellation bookkeeping in full and notes where the lid's integrability is spent — twice, once per cancellation, neither optional.

Two riders complete the jewel's papers, both desk-proved tonight. The convergence is stronger than stated: not only do the integrals converge — the integral of the absolute discrepancy converges to nought; run the double valve on the discrepancies themselves, dominated by twice the lid, and the limit-in-the-mean drops out, a phrase Episode Six will formalize into a geometry. And the lid's own integral bounds everything in sight uniformly, so the limit inherits integrability with room to spare — the desk's bookkeeping makes both riders two lines each.

Let the wonder beat sound here, sir, as the plan designates, and let it be the quiet kind. There is no new machinery in that proof. The staircases built the integral; the crankshaft turned the climb; the climb proved the valve; the valve, doubled, proved the jewel. Four evenings of this season, stacked in a single column, and at the top — the theorem that every working analyst, every probabilist, every engineer who has ever differentiated under an integral sign or swapped an expectation with a limit, uses more often than any other single result of twentieth-century mathematics. It is the season's whole argument, sir, compressed into one licensing clause: measure the ground honestly, and the limits move free.

---

### The Bounded Corollary

One special case deserves its own name before the applications, because it is the form your trade meets daily and the form that retires a Season One theorem with honours. On finite ground — the unit interval, any frame, any probability space — a constant is integrable; so if a pointwise-convergent sequence is uniformly bounded — one number capping every term everywhere — the constant is a lid, and the jewel applies: the bounded convergence theorem, domination's pocket edition. Probability lives on ground of measure one, sir, so this corollary is the workhorse of Episode Eight's entire subject: bounded random quantities swap limits and expectations without further ceremony. And note its reach backward: Season One's finale proved the uniform-convergence interchange theorem with a page of tube bookkeeping; tonight it is two lines — uniform convergence on the finite interval eventually bounds the sequence by the limit's bound plus one, a constant lid, done. The finale's theorem was the pocket edition's pocket edition, sir; the season's machinery re-proves its ancestor in passing, which is how one knows the machinery is the right one.

---

### What the Lid Buys

Three applications with teeth, in ascending order of your likely affection.

First: series of signed terms. Check the absolute series integrates — Tonelli-for-series, the nonnegative freedom of the credit's corollary — and the lid is the absolute partial sums' majorant; dominated convergence swaps sum and integral. The standard operating procedure, now fully licensed on the line.

Second: continuity of integrals in a parameter. An integral depending on a dial — a temperature, a time, a hyperparameter — is continuous in the dial wherever the integrand is continuous in it and dominated uniformly in it: take any sequence of dial settings converging to a target, and the lid marches the limit through. One integrable roof, checked once; continuity everywhere under it.

Third, the celebrated one: differentiation under the integral sign. If the integrand's partial derivative in the dial exists and is itself dominated — one integrable lid over all the difference quotients' witnesses, which the mean value theorem of Season One supplies from a lid on the derivative — then the derivative of the integral is the integral of the derivative. The desk states the hypotheses with full precision and proves the theorem by exactly the sequence-plus-lid manoeuvre above. This, sir, is the trick your trade attributes to Feynman — he learned it, by his own cheerful account, from a calculus text nobody else had read, and wielded it as a private superpower; it is licensed tonight as a two-line corollary of the crown jewel, and the desk sets one specimen integral for sport, with the honesty clause noting its logarithm still rides on Season One's credit. Feynman's superpower, sir, was this season's Episode Five, read early.

---

### The Parade of Counterexamples

The licenses earn their fine print, per the plan's own mandate: each hypothesis violated, once, in public.

Monotone convergence without monotonicity: the bump — nonnegative, pointwise to zero, integrals stuck at one; the climb was the load-bearing clause. Monotone convergence climbing from the wrong side: descending sequences with infinite starts — one over x above n, say, descending to zero with every integral infinite — the theorem's mirror needs a finite first floor, exactly as the crankshaft's shrinking chains did, and the desk files the kinship. Fatou without the sign: allow negatives and mass can be created — the negative spike, minus n on ground one over n, has integrals minus one and liminf zero; the valve leaks backward without its nonnegativity gasket. Dominated convergence without the lid: all three escapes, each individually fatal, as computed. And the spread once more, for emphasis: uniform convergence, no lid, swap fails — uniformity neither implies domination nor substitutes for it. Five violations, five failures, no theorem wounded: the hypotheses, sir, are not lawyer's caution; each is a wall against a named escape.

---

### The Account, Closed

The register, sir, and tonight it closes the oldest active account in the establishment.

Debt five: the swap account. Opened, Season One, Episode Four, at the rearrangement outrage, with the words: when may two limiting processes be exchanged? Instalment one, Season One, Episode Seven: limits past limits, the uniform license, Cauchy's corpse as exhibit. Instalment two, the season finale: limit past integral, uniformity again, the moving spike convicted, the stinginess codicil filed with the payment. Instalment three, tonight: the crown jewels — climbing mass swaps free; nonnegative mass swaps free; dominated mass swaps free; and the fine print is three pictures long. The account is closed, sir — not paid off and forgotten, but closed the way a good account closes: converted into standing law. I read the closing comparison into the record. Season One's license: uniform control at every point, finite ground, and even then the theorems came one at a time. This season's: one integrable lid — or mere monotonicity, or mere nonnegativity — and the swaps hold on any measurable ground in the building, infinite included. The stinginess codicil is discharged with prejudice. Two seasons, sir, from outrage to law; the register notes that no account has travelled further or arrived better.

The bell: silent tonight, and the silence is the elegant kind — the count holds at sixteen. Every theorem of the evening ran on ring sixteen's supremum, the crankshaft's swelling chains, and the staircases — instruments long since paid for. When a season's crown jewels ring nothing new, sir, the season's architecture is finished; what remains is furniture.

## Episode S2·E6 — The Zoo of Convergence, or Littlewood's Three Principles

#### The Measure of All Things, Season Two, Episode Six

### The Field Guide

Good day, sir.

John Edensor Littlewood — Hardy's collaborator, Trinity's resident sceptic, and a man whose working maxims have outlived most other men's theorems — claimed that the whole of this season's subject reduces to three heuristics, and I shall read them as our field guide tonight. Every measurable set is nearly a finite union of intervals. Every measurable function is nearly continuous. Every convergent sequence of measurable functions is nearly uniformly convergent. Three sentences, sir — and the word doing all the work in each is nearly. Not approximately, not morally: nearly, in the exact currency this season mints — off a set of measure as small as you please. Tonight the establishment takes inventory after last week's summit: five modes of convergence now circulate on the premises, and we shall sort the entire menagerie — which modes imply which, which extract which along subsequences, and which counterexamples keep every arrow honest — then give Littlewood's second and third principles their formal names, Lusin and Egorov, and close with a structure the twentieth century built from tonight's materials: the space whose points are functions and whose distance is an integral. The first principle, you will recognize, was banked two episodes... four episodes ago, at the approximation manners; tonight completes the trilogy.

---

### The Five Modes

The cast, introduced in one breath apiece, each with its character.

Uniform convergence you have known since Season One, Episode Seven: one tube, every point inside, the aristocrat's mode — expensive and unbending. Pointwise convergence, likewise of long acquaintance: every point settles, each at its own pace, no coordination — the mode that shattered continuity and taught the course to fear. Almost-everywhere convergence, the amnesty's child: pointwise off a null set — pointwise, as this season prices things, with the clerical noise discarded. Convergence in the mean: the integral of the discrepancy tends to nought — last week's rider, now promoted to a mode in its own right; the sequence and its limit agree in total mass of disagreement, wherever that disagreement sits. And the newcomer, convergence in measure: for every tolerance, the ground on which the discrepancy exceeds the tolerance shrinks to nothing — not the size of the disagreement but the acreage of it, sent to zero. The statistician's mode, sir, and your trade's: convergence in probability is this mode wearing next week's... the finale's costume, and every consistency proof you have ever cited lives here.

---

### The Modes in the Wild

Before the map, a word on why five modes exist at all, since the zoo can look like taxonomy for its own sake. Each mode, sir, is the natural currency of a different working question. Uniform convergence is the numericist's guarantee: one error bound, valid across the whole domain — the tabulated function trusted everywhere at once, Season One's grid-table certificate. Almost-everywhere convergence is the trajectory-watcher's mode: fix the sample path, follow it forever — the strong law of large numbers, when the finale states it, will speak this dialect. Convergence in the mean is the auditor's: total expected error, mass of mistake — the loss your trade actually minimizes, integrated over the data. And convergence in measure — in probability, on mass-one ground — is the statistician's: the chance of a noticeable error vanishes, nothing said about totals or trajectories; every consistency theorem in your libraries speaks it. Five questions, five currencies; the map that follows is the exchange-rate table, and the counterexamples are the exchange's posted warnings.

---

### The Geography

Now the map — what lies upstream of what — narrated as geography and drawn properly at the desk, with a proof or a counterexample on every arrow, no exceptions.

Uniform sits at the headwaters: it implies pointwise, hence almost-everywhere, trivially; on finite ground it implies the mean — the tube's cross-section times a finite width — and thence in-measure. Downstream, the mean implies measure always, by an argument you should hear once, for it is one line and your trade calls it by name: the ground where the discrepancy exceeds epsilon contributes at least epsilon times its own acreage to the integral, so the acreage is at most the integral over epsilon. Mass bounds acreage — Chebyshev's inequality in embryo, sir; the finale will christen it properly, and it is the map's most-travelled road. Almost-everywhere implies in-measure on finite ground — a dividend of Egorov, presently — and fails without finiteness: the marching bump converges at every point, yet its discrepancy-acreage holds at one forever; the horizon exit again, closed to it last week by lids, open to it tonight because no lid is asked. Walk the arrows once, sir, compass in hand. From uniform: south to pointwise, southeast (on finite ground) to the mean; every road out of uniform is paved. From pointwise: south to almost-everywhere, and no road east — the spike blocks the way to the mean. From the mean: east to in-measure, always, by Chebyshev's embryo. From almost-everywhere: east to in-measure on finite ground only — the bump patrols the unbounded frontier. And from in-measure: no road back west to almost-everywhere — the typewriter stands athwart it — save the subsequence bridle-path, presently. Every other pairing is a composition of these or a counterexample; the desk's diagram carries the complete table, every cell warranted. And the mean and almost-everywhere, sir, imply each other in neither direction — the gallery's two prize beasts each break one arrow. The spike converges to zero almost everywhere while its mean discrepancy holds at one: pointwise settlement, mass unsurrendered. The other direction's beast deserves its own section, and a moment of theatre besides, for I have been saving it since the season was planned.

---

### The Typewriter

Watch, sir — I shall narrate it slowly, as it deserves.

Take the unit interval. The first function: the indicator of the whole interval — one block, full width. Then two blocks, each of width one half: the indicator of the left half; then of the right half. Then four blocks of width one quarter, sweeping left to right: first quarter, second, third, fourth. Then eight blocks of width one eighth, sweeping again; then sixteen; and so on forever — each generation halving the block and sweeping the interval end to end, like a typewriter's carriage: type across the line, return, halve the type, type across again. That is the sequence — the typewriter — and I ask two questions of it.

Where does it converge in measure, and in the mean? Everywhere, and emphatically: the n-th block's width — its supporting acreage, and equally its integral — is one over two to the k at generation k, and generations advance forever; discrepancy-acreage and discrepancy-mass alike march to zero. By both of the integral-flavoured modes, the typewriter converges to the zero function, and rapidly.

And where does it converge pointwise? Nowhere, sir. Not at one single point of the interval. Fix any point you please: every generation's carriage sweeps the whole interval, so every generation sends exactly one block across your point — the function reads one there, once per generation, forever; and between visits it reads nought. At your point — at every point — the sequence reads nought, nought, one, nought, one, nought, nought, one, without end: infinitely many ones, infinitely many noughts, no settlement, no limit. A sequence converging to zero in measure and in mean, and converging pointwise at no point whatsoever.

Let the wonder beat sound here, for this is the evening's designated moment and the finest convergence counterexample in the literature. The two families of modes, sir, are measuring different things, and the typewriter is the proof that neither family reports to the other. The integral modes watch the mass and the acreage of disagreement: both vanish, and those modes are satisfied — the disagreement never lingers anywhere. The pointwise modes stand at a fixed address and demand the visits stop: they never do; the carriage always returns. Smallness of the offence and persistence of the offence are different failures — the typewriter offends infinitely often, each time more briefly; total offence vanishing, offence at every address eternal. Season One taught you that a function's behaviour at points and its behaviour in bulk could diverge; the typewriter is that lesson promoted to sequences, and it is, I submit, a perfect ear-object: you can hear the carriage return.

---

### The Consolation Prize

The typewriter breaks the arrow from measure to almost-everywhere; here is what survives of it, and it suffices surprisingly often.

Convergence in measure extracts almost-everywhere convergence along a subsequence. The strategy is the season's signature gambit in its purest form. From the in-measure hypothesis, harvest a fast subsequence: a first index where the epsilon-half discrepancy-ground is smaller than one half; a later index where the quarter-ground is under a quarter; a later still where the eighth-ground is under an eighth — the k-th chosen index confining its two-to-the-k discrepancy to acreage under two to the minus k. Now total the acreages beyond any stage: a geometric tail, as small as you please; so the points visited by infinitely many of the confined discrepancy-grounds form a null set — trapped under tails of every size. Off that null set, every point is eventually clear of the grounds, and the fast subsequence settles within every tolerance: almost-everywhere convergence, extracted. The typewriter illustrates rather than resists: its generations' first blocks — widths one, one half, one quarter — form exactly such a fast subsequence, converging to zero at every point except the left endpoint, a set of one. And I flag, for the finale, the argument's skeleton: summable acreages force finitely many visits almost surely — the course will meet it there under its proper name, the first Borel–Cantelli lemma, and you will have proved it tonight without being told.

---
### Egorov's Theorem

Littlewood's third principle, made rigorous — and note that it is the principle the typewriter appears to mock: every convergent sequence is nearly uniformly convergent. The typewriter converges pointwise nowhere, so the principle owes it nothing; the principle speaks of sequences that do converge, and about those it says something remarkable.

Egorov's theorem, nineteen eleven. On ground of finite measure, if a sequence of measurable functions converges almost everywhere, then for every epsilon there is a citizen set, occupying all but epsilon of the ground, on which the convergence is uniform. Uniform, sir — the aristocrat's mode, Season One's expensive license — purchased on almost all the ground for an epsilon of sacrificed acreage. Pointwise convergence, the mode that shattered continuity, is uniform convergence wearing a threadbare patch: cut out a set as small as you please, and the tube closes around everything that remains.

The proof strategy fits in the ear, and it is two of this season's instruments in sequence. For a fixed tolerance — one over k — consider the bad tails: the ground where some discrepancy beyond stage n still exceeds the tolerance. As n grows these bad tails shrink, and they shrink to nothing — almost-everywhere convergence says almost no point stays bad forever — so the shrinking crankshaft, on finite ground with its finite first floor, sends their measures to zero: some stage confines the k-tolerance offenders to acreage under epsilon over two to the k. Do this for every k and spend the gambit: total sacrificed acreage under epsilon, and on the remainder every tolerance is met uniformly beyond its stage — which is uniform convergence, certificate in hand. Shrinking crankshaft plus the epsilon-over-two-to-the-k gambit; the desk writes it in full, and marks where finite ground is spent — the crankshaft's finite floor — with the marching bump as the standing witness that the clause is real: on the infinite line, the bump converges everywhere and is uniform on no cofinite-measure set; its escape is exactly the crankshaft's caveat at work.

---

### Lusin's Theorem

Littlewood's second principle: every measurable function is nearly continuous. Formally — Lusin, nineteen twelve: a measurable function, finite almost everywhere on a frame, admits, for every epsilon, a closed set occupying all but epsilon of the frame on which the function's restriction is continuous. The monsters of two seasons, sir — the static, Thomae's creature, anything the tribe can weigh — are continuous functions in disguise, the disguise being a set of acreage epsilon; respectable citizens, almost.

Two footnotes give the theorem its exact edges. Continuity of the restriction, sir, not continuity at the points: the static restricted to the irrationals is identically nought — continuous as a function on that set — though the static is continuous at no point of the line; Lusin promises the former, never the latter, and the distinction is worth a pin through it. And the theorem characterizes: a function with Lusin's property — nearly continuous at every epsilon — is necessarily measurable, so the principle is an exact portrait of the tribe, not merely a courtesy it extends. The proof is an assembly of the season's parts, and the episode gives the assembly order while the desk gives the references and the sketch, per the plan's own budget: staircase-approximate the function by simple functions; each simple function is nearly continuous — its storeys' citizens are nearly finite unions of intervals, the first principle, banked at the approximation manners; the staircases converge almost everywhere, so Egorov — tonight's own theorem — makes the convergence nearly uniform; and a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, Season One's three-legged stool, still load-bearing two seasons on. Nearly, plus nearly, plus Egorov's nearly, the epsilons split by the gambit: three sacrifices, each as small as you please, and the closed certificate emerges from the regularity manners. All three of Littlewood's principles, sir, are one epsilon-management discipline viewed from three angles — sets, functions, sequences — and tonight the trilogy stands assembled, each principle citing the others' paperwork.

---

### The Mean as a Distance

The last movement opens a door the course will not walk through, but the doorway itself is one of the twentieth century's load-bearing arches, and this season built every stone of it.

Consider the integrable functions on a fixed ground, and declare the distance between two of them to be the integral of their absolute discrepancy — the mean distance. Convergence in the mean is exactly convergence in this distance; the amnesty becomes geometry — functions equal almost everywhere stand at distance zero, so the space's honest points are the equivalence classes, functions-up-to-clerical-noise, precisely the objects Episode Four said the theory works with; and the triangle inequality is the additivity of the integral applied to a pointwise triangle. A space, sir, whose points are functions and whose geometry is integration: the trade calls it L-one, and its younger siblings — the L-p family, distances built from p-th powers, your trade's regularizers among them — are glimpsed at the desk with their nesting on finite ground.

And the theorem that makes the space an instrument rather than a curiosity: it is complete. Every sequence of integrable functions that huddles in the mean — Cauchy in the mean distance, Season One's dialect — converges in the mean to an integrable limit. Riesz and Fischer, nineteen oh seven — two proofs, independent, the same year, and both, fittingly, in papers about Fourier series: the account that opened this course funding, once again, the mathematics that answers it. And the bell, sir — ring the seventeenth, and I cite the precedent with the ceremony: ring twelve, the first ever inked off the real line, rang for the completeness of the space of continuous functions under the uniform distance; tonight its exact successor — the completeness of the space of integrable functions under the mean distance — and the proof is this season's machinery entire, conducted at the desk as the guided centrepiece: extract a fast subsequence by the gambit; stack its discrepancies into a nonnegative series; the climbing license prices the stack integrable; its finiteness almost everywhere hands the subsequence an almost-everywhere limit; and the dominated jewel — lid supplied by the stack — closes the huddle onto the limit in the mean. Every jewel of last week, spent once, in order. The count stands at seventeen, flagged for veto as its predecessors were; the axiom of completeness, having built the line, the integral of Season One, and the integral of Season Two, now certifies the space in which twentieth-century analysis actually lives. Hilbert's spectral theory, Fourier's account at its eventual settlement, the function spaces of your trade's optimizers — all tenants, sir, of the arch completed tonight.

---

### The Exiles

Two inequalities remain, and I shall treat them exactly as the plan directs — named, motivated, and exiled to paper by name — because they are the standing example of this course's ear-and-desk discipline, and I say so, sir, on the record, as the plan instructs me to.

Hölder's inequality: the integral of a product is bounded by the product of conjugate-power norms — the reason products of integrable things integrate, the engine of every duality your trade's optimization theory runs on. Minkowski's inequality: the triangle inequality for the whole L-p family — the reason the p-distances are distances at all. Each is motivated in one sentence, as I have just done; each is proved at the desk properly, via Young's inequality with the calculus conducted in full; and neither will be narrated further aloud, because each is precisely the species of epsilon-and-exponent management that the ear cannot hold and was never asked to. Named, motivated, exiled. The discipline of two seasons, sir, in its purest specimen: the honest division of labour is not a compromise; it is the design.

---

### The Season's Ledger

The register. Rung: the bell, once — ring seventeen, Riesz and Fischer, the mean distance's completeness, on the precedent of ring twelve; flagged for veto; the count stands at seventeen. Banked: the implication map entire, every arrow proved or convicted at the desk — the typewriter, the spike, the bump, and the spread each holding down their corners; the subsequence consolation with its Borel–Cantelli skeleton flagged for the finale; Egorov and Lusin, Littlewood's trilogy assembled. Standing: Fourier's account — the arch of the mean distance is, historically and mathematically, the room where that account settles; the desk's notes say where the course's boundary lies and what one further season would collect. And the establishment notes, sir, with a certain satisfaction: two episodes remain, and every instrument the finale requires is now on the premises.

---

### Terms of Engagement

The desk's half of the evening — chapter six of the second volume — toured in the standing manner.

The notation ledger seats the five modes with their formal definitions, the mean distance, the fast-subsequence notation, and the conjugate exponents.

Proofs in full: the implication diagram — every arrow of the map proved or refuted, the chapter's core, with the four beasts stationed at their corners and the finite-ground clauses marked where they bite; the Chebyshev-in-embryo estimate; the typewriter formalized, both convergences computed and the pointwise-nowhere verdict proved at every point; the subsequence-extraction lemma with the gambit and the tail-trap displayed; Egorov entire, the shrinking crankshaft's finite floor cited at its line; the mean distance's metric axioms with the amnesty-as-geometry remark; and Riesz–Fischer as the guided centrepiece, solved in full — the fast subsequence, the stacked series, the climbing license, the dominated closure, each jewel's citation at its point of expenditure. ### Until Next Time

The ledger's summary lines, sir: one ring, on precedent; the map complete; the trilogy assembled; the exiles honoured; the arch of the mean distance standing. Two episodes remain.

For next time: the crime of swapping integrals themselves. Every engineer, every physicist, every practitioner of your trade has exchanged the order of a double integral — integrated over x, then t, and trusted the answer to match the other itinerary — without a second thought. Episode Seven determines exactly when that manoeuvre is licensed and when it is a crime with consequences: the plane's measure built honestly from the line's — the product construction, with the dimension license of Episode Two finally cashed in full; Tonelli's theorem — for nonnegative functions, swap freely, always, the standard operating procedure's first commandment; Fubini's theorem — for integrable functions, swap after checking the absolute integral, the second commandment; and the crime scene itself — a function on the unit square, elegant as you please, whose two iterated integrals both exist and disagree, the desk computing both to the digit. ## Episode S2·E7 — Fubini, or the Crime of Swapping Integrals

#### The Measure of All Things, Season Two, Episode Seven

### The Manoeuvre

Good day, sir.

There is a manoeuvre so habitual in the quantitative trades that most practitioners no longer notice performing it. A quantity depends on two variables; one integrates over both; and one chooses — without ceremony, without a second thought — the order of the itinerary: sweep x first and then t, or t first and then x, confident the answer cannot care about the bookkeeping. Every double sum in your libraries, every expectation of an expectation, every marginalization in every probabilistic model you have ever shipped, is this manoeuvre. Tonight, sir, the establishment determines exactly when it is a licensed operation and when it is a crime with consequences — and I use the word crime advisedly, because tonight's exhibits include a function, elegant as you please, whose two itineraries both complete successfully and return different answers. Not divergence, not breakdown: two finite numbers, computed correctly, disagreeing. The desk will compute both to the digit, and the diagnosis will be an old acquaintance wearing new dress.

The programme: first the plane itself, built honestly — the season has measured the line; tonight the product construction measures the plane from two copies of it, and the dimension license of Episode Two is cashed in full, from both sides. Then the two commandments, a matched pair: Tonelli's theorem — for nonnegative functions, swap freely, always, even to infinity; and Fubini's theorem — for integrable functions, swap after checking the absolute integral. Then the crime scene, with the fine print about sigma-finiteness that even careful practitioners forget exists. And at the close, the dividend the plan bills as the bridge to how probabilists think: the layer cake — an integral recomputed as the area under the distribution of its heights — with which the two seasons' notions of integration shake hands one final time before the finale. To work.

---

### The Plane, Built from the Line

The plane must be measured before it can host integrals, and there are two honest routes to its measure. Route one you have owned since Episode Two: run the whole season's construction directly in two dimensions — rectangles for intervals, countable rectangle covers, the same infimum, Carathéodory's same criterion; the dimension license, verbatim. Route two is tonight's, and it is the structurally interesting one: build the plane's measure as a product of two lines, because the product construction is what generalizes — to the product of any two measure spaces whatsoever, your trade's joint distributions included, where no ambient geometry exists to run route one.

The product construction in three breaths. The measurable rectangles: products of a citizen of the first line with a citizen of the second — the atoms of two-dimensional bookkeeping, priced at length times length, the schoolroom's area rule promoted to a definition. The product sigma-algebra: the tribe the rectangles generate — the smallest sigma-algebra containing them, existence by the intersection-from-above construction of this season's first evening, working its third season of service. And the product measure: extend the rectangle pricing to the whole tribe — by Carathéodory's machinery run on rectangle covers, exactly as the line ran on interval covers; the theorem of nineteen fourteen was proved once and serves forever, which was always its advertisement. Uniqueness comes from the same well: two contract-keepers agreeing on rectangles agree on the tribe, by the frame-squeeze of Episode Two transplanted. And the two routes agree, sir — the direct plane measure and the product measure coincide on their common jurisdiction — the desk proving agreement on rectangles and letting uniqueness carry the rest. One plane, one measure, two derivations; the books close.

One vocabulary item completes the toolkit: sections. Fix a height y, and any set in the plane casts a shadow at that height — the x-section, the set of x whose pair lies in the set; dually the y-sections. A function of two variables, frozen at one height, becomes a function of one — the section functions. The x-knife and the y-knife, sir: the two ways of carving a planar object into linear slices, and the entire subject of iterated integration is the accounting relationship between a planar whole and its two families of slices. The foundational lemma — every section of a product-measurable set is measurable on its line; every section of a product-measurable function is measurable — is proved at the desk, with a candour I flag now: its full proof wants an induction over the tribe's generation that the trade calls a monotone-class argument, and the plan directs me to flag that machinery honestly rather than smuggle it. The desk states the monotone-class lemma, proves the accessible half, and cites the standard shelves for the remainder — the season's one borrowed beam, clearly labelled.

---

### Tonelli's Theorem

The first commandment, sir — Leonida Tonelli, nineteen oh nine — and it is the nonnegative freedom of Episode Five grown up to two dimensions.

For a nonnegative measurable function on the product: the double integral — the merchant's count run on the plane's measure directly — equals the iterated integral, x first then y, and equals the iterated integral, y first then x. All three, always, with no hypothesis beyond the sign — and "always" includes infinity: if any one of the three is infinite, all three are, in honest agreement. Nonnegativity is the universal license. Mass that cannot cancel cannot conspire: sweep it in any order and the total is the total.

The proof is this season's greatest-hits reel, and I narrate its architecture with some pride of ownership. Stage one: rectangles — for the indicator of a rectangle, all three integrals read length times length by inspection. Stage two: from rectangles to the tribe — the monotone-class beam carries indicator agreement from the generating atoms to every product-measurable set; here sits the borrowed machinery, spent exactly once. Stage three: from indicators to everything — the staircase of the range lifts indicator agreement to simple functions by linearity, and the climbing license lifts simple agreement to all nonnegative measurable functions, staircases ascending under all three integrals at once, monotone convergence passing the limit through each. Rectangles, tribe, staircases, climb: every load-bearing wall is an instrument this season built, and the theorem that licenses your marginalizations is, at bottom, the observation that all three ways of counting agree on rectangles and that everything else is a limit of rectangles. 

---

### Fubini's Theorem

The second commandment — Guido Fubini, nineteen oh seven — handles signs, and its statement carries the check that gives the standard operating procedure its shape.

For an integrable function on the product — integrable, meaning the absolute value's double integral is finite — the two iterated integrals exist, agree, and equal the double integral. The inner integrals, I note for precision, exist for almost every value of the outer variable — a null set of bad slices is tolerated and absorbed, the amnesty working its passage even here. The proof, once Tonelli stands, is bookkeeping of a familiar shape: split into gains and losses, apply Tonelli to each — both finite, by the integrability check — and subtract, every term lawful.

And so the doctrine, sir, stated as doctrine — the standard operating procedure, promised in Episode Five, canonized tonight. To swap a double integral: if the integrand is nonnegative, swap freely — Tonelli, no questions asked. If the integrand carries signs, first run Tonelli on its absolute value — a nonnegative computation, itself swappable at will — and if that absolute total is finite, swap the original freely — Fubini; if infinite, do not swap — you are outside the license, and the crime scene ahead shows what the territory looks like. One checks with Tonelli and spends with Fubini. That procedure, sir, executed reflexively for a century by everyone who computes, is the entire content of the matched pair — and note the family resemblance to Season One's series doctrine: absolute convergence licensed rearrangement; conditional convergence forbade it; the plane's integrals obey the same constitution, because they are the same phenomenon — an uncountable rearrangement question, wearing area's clothes.

---

### The Crime Scene

Now the exhibit, sir, and I shall describe it geometrically before the desk computes it, because the geometry is the diagnosis.

On the quarter-plane — x and y from nought to infinity — build a staircase of blocks along the diagonal: on each unit square sitting on the diagonal — corners at whole numbers, the k-th square spanning k to k plus one in both coordinates — place mass plus one, spread uniformly; and give each such block a shadow: mass minus one on the square immediately to its right — same storey, next column, just below the diagonal. A staircase of positive blocks, each casting a negative shadow one column rightward. That is the whole function: plus-one blocks on the diagonal, minus-one blocks just under it, nought elsewhere — bounded, measurable, elementary as furniture.

Run the y-itinerary first: fix a column — a vertical line at position x — and total what the column sees. A column through the k-th unit of x, for k at least one, passes through exactly two blocks: its own storey's positive block on the diagonal, and the shadow cast into it by the storey below — one plus, one minus, total nought. But the very first column — x below one — meets the ground floor's positive block and no shadow at all: the ground floor casts its shadow into the second column, and no storey exists below to cast one back. Column totals: one on the first unit of x, nought forever after. Integrate over x: one.

Now the x-itinerary: fix a row — a horizontal line at height y — and sweep across. The row through the k-th storey meets that storey's positive block on the diagonal and that same storey's shadow, parked one column to the right — both present for every storey, the ground floor included, since every block casts its shadow sideways rather than downward. One plus, one minus: every row totals nought, without exception. Integrate over y: nought.

One itinerary returns one; the other returns nought. Both computations are finite, elementary, and correct — the desk performs each to the digit, block by block — and they disagree. No error has been made, sir; the manoeuvre itself is the error. Run the check the doctrine demands and the diagnosis appears at once: the absolute value of this function is a one on every block, positive and shadow alike — an infinite staircase of unit masses — and its double integral is infinite. The integrability check fails; Fubini's license was never issued; and the two itineraries are two conditionally convergent rearrangements of the same signed mass, each converging to its own answer — the Riemann rearrangement theorem of Season One, Episode Four, staged on the quarter-plane with blocks for terms. The crime was never exotic, sir. It is the oldest crime in the course, in two dimensions.

---

### The Fine Print

One clause remains, easy to forget and cheap to state. Both commandments assume the two measure spaces are sigma-finite — coverable by countably many pieces of finite measure, the clerical property the line has enjoyed since Episode Two's frames and the season filed as fine print with an appointment for tonight. Drop it and even Tonelli fails: the standard witness pairs the unit interval under ordinary length with the unit interval under counting measure — every set priced by its number of points, an honest measure with no countable finite cover — and examines the indicator of the diagonal. One itinerary integrates to nought, the other to one; nonnegative, measurable, and disagreeing, because the counting side is too vast for rectangle bookkeeping to approximate. The desk files the computation in three lines. The moral for practice is brief: every space your trade will ever integrate over is sigma-finite, and the clause costs you nothing — but the theorems' statements carry it, and now you know which exhibit put it there.

---

### The Layer Cake

The dividend, sir — the plan calls it the bridge to how probabilists think, and it has been my favourite application of Tonelli since I learned the trade.

Take a nonnegative measurable function on any sigma-finite ground. For each height t above nought, ask: how much ground does the function exceed t upon? — the acreage of the pile above t, a decreasing function of the height; the season's oldest question, asked at every altitude at once. The layer-cake representation: the integral of the function equals the integral, over all heights, of those acreages. Total mass equals the accumulated area of the horizontal slices — the cake priced layer by layer rather than column by column.

The proof is Tonelli performing a somersault, and it fits in the ear entire. Consider, on the product of the ground with the half-line of heights, the indicator of the region under the graph — one when the height is below the function's value, nought otherwise. Integrate heights first, ground second: at each point of the ground, the inner integral measures the heights beneath the function's value there — which is the value itself; the outer integral then totals the function: the left side. Integrate ground first, heights second: at each height, the inner integral measures the ground where the function exceeds the height — the acreage of the pile; the outer integral accumulates the acreages: the right side. One region, two itineraries, both nonnegative — Tonelli licenses the equality without conditions, and the identity drops out. The subgraph, sliced vertically, is the integral; sliced horizontally, it is the distribution of heights. Your trade, sir, lives on the horizontal slicing: every tail-probability computation, every expected value written as an integral of survival probabilities, every quantile argument, is the layer cake — the finale will write expectation equals the integral of the tail probabilities, and it will be tonight's identity wearing its proper uniform. The merchant of Episode Four sorted the till by denomination; the layer cake prices the till by cumulative solvency; and the two seasons' pictures of an integral — area under a curve, mass sorted by value — meet in the subgraph, which is both at once. The wonder beat of the evening, sir, spends itself on that handshake.

---

The register. The bell: silent, count holding at seventeen — the product measure ran Carathéodory's staircase a second time and priced its books with instruments long since rung; a construction that repeats itself is architecture, not news. Canonized: the standard operating procedure — check with Tonelli, spend with Fubini — the small promise of Episode Five discharged. Borrowed, labelled, and shelved: the monotone-class beam, the season's one import, cited with its shelf-mark at the desk. Convicted: the staircase-and-shadows function, the quarter-plane's rearrangement criminal; and the diagonal under counting measure, the fine print's witness. Banked: the layer cake, with the finale's tail-probability identity pre-signed. Standing: Fourier's account, one evening from settlement day; and the finale's full slate — the dictionary, the laws of large numbers, the bridge to your desk — with every instrument now on the premises. One episode remains, sir.

The desk's half of the evening — chapter seven of the second volume — toured in the standing manner.

The notation ledger seats the rectangles, the product tribe and measure, the sections with both knives, the iterated-integral notations, and the subgraph.
