*On the extended nonnegative reals (the ledger's fine print).* — Outer measure takes values in $[0, \infty]$: the symbol $\infty$ is admitted as an honest verdict, with the arithmetic $a + \infty = \infty$ and $a \le \infty$ for all $a$, and one standing prohibition — $\infty - \infty$ is never written, and no argument of this season will need it (Remark 1.8). Series of nonnegative terms converge or diverge to $\infty$ with no third possibility (Volume One, the monotone license, Chapter 4); every sum below is of this kind.

#### 1.2 The Contract

> **Definition 1.1 (The contract for a length).** A candidate notion of length is an assignment $\mu$ of a value in $[0, \infty]$ to sets of reals (all sets, or a declared tribe of them), demanded to satisfy:
>
> 1. **(i)** $\mu(\emptyset) = 0$;
> 1. **(ii)** $\mu(I) = b - a$ for every interval $I$ with endpoints $a \le b$, open, closed, or half-open;
> 1. **(iii)** (translation invariance) $\mu(A + t) = \mu(A)$ for every $t \in \R$, where $A + t = \{ a + t : a \in A \}$;
> 1. **(iv)** (countable additivity) for every sequence $A_1, A_2, \dots$ of pairwise disjoint sets in the domain whose union is in the domain, $\mu\bigl( \bigcup_k A_k \bigr) = \sum_k \mu(A_k)$.
>
> Finite additivity is the weakening of (iv) to finitely many pieces; it follows from (iv) by padding with empty sets, clause (i) absorbing the padding.

> **Remark 1.2 (Additivity across arbitrary families is not on the table).** $[0,1]$ is the disjoint union of its singletons. Each singleton has length zero under any candidate honouring (ii) and monotone common sense: $\{x\} \subseteq (x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon)$ for every $\varepsilon$. An additivity clause surviving uncountable disassembly would price $[0,1]$ as a "sum" of uncountably many zeros; no convention for such sums yields one (any reasonable definition — say, the supremum of finite subsums — yields zero). Clause (iv) stops at countable by necessity, not modesty.

> **Proposition 1.3 (Continuity of measure — the engine's crankshaft).** Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a sigma-algebra and $\mu$ a countably additive assignment on $\mathcal{A}$ with values in $[0,\infty]$ and $\mu(\emptyset) = 0$. (This proposition is stated for the tribes to come; from Chapter 2 onward it is used constantly.)
>
> 1. **(i)** (Swelling chains) If $A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \cdots$, all in $\mathcal{A}$, then $\mu\bigl( \bigcup_n A_n \bigr) = \lim_n \mu(A_n)$.
> 1. **(ii)** (Shrinking chains) If $A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq \cdots$, all in $\mathcal{A}$, and $\mu(A_1) < \infty$, then $\mu\bigl( \bigcap_n A_n \bigr) = \lim_n \mu(A_n)$. The finiteness hypothesis is not removable: $A_n = [n, \infty)$ shrinks to the empty set with every $\mu(A_n)$ infinite (once Chapter 2 delivers the measure, this is a lawful exhibit; the Archimedean property of Volume One, Theorem 2.12, empties the intersection).

*Proof.* (i) Disjointify into rings of growth: $B_1 = A_1$ and $B_k = A_k \setminus A_{k-1}$ for $k \ge 2$. Each $B_k$ lies in $\mathcal{A}$ (complement and intersection, via De Morgan); the $B_k$ are pairwise disjoint; $\bigcup_{k \le n} B_k = A_n$; and $\bigcup_k B_k = \bigcup_n A_n$. Countable additivity prices the union as $\sum_k \mu(B_k)$, whose partial sums are, by finite additivity, $\mu(A_n)$ — the telescope, Volume One's oldest cancellation. A series of nonnegative terms *is* the limit of its partial sums: $\mu(\bigcup A_n) = \lim \mu(A_n)$.

(ii) Pass to complements within $A_1$: the sets $A_1 \setminus A_n$ swell to $A_1 \setminus \bigcap_n A_n$. Apply (i), then subtract from $\mu(A_1)$ — lawful precisely because $\mu(A_1) < \infty$ keeps every quantity finite and the prohibited $\infty - \infty$ off the page (finite additivity gives $\mu(A_1) = \mu(A_n) + \mu(A_1 \setminus A_n)$, so $\mu(A_1 \setminus A_n) = \mu(A_1) - \mu(A_n)$, and likewise for the intersection). The identity rearranges to the claim. The converse direction — (i) plus finite additivity recovers countable additivity — is Problem II.2, solved in full: the engine and the clause are one mechanism. ∎

#### 1.3 Jordan's Content

> **Definition 1.4 (Inner and outer content).** For bounded $A \subseteq \R$: the *inner content* $\underline{c}(A)$ is the supremum of $\sum_{j=1}^{N} \lvert I_j \rvert$ over all *finite* families of pairwise disjoint intervals with $\bigcup_j I_j \subseteq A$; the *outer content* $\overline{c}(A)$ is the infimum of $\sum_{j=1}^{N} \lvert I_j \rvert$ over all finite families with $A \subseteq \bigcup_j I_j$. Always $\underline{c}(A) \le \overline{c}(A)$; when equal, $A$ is *Jordan measurable* with content the common value.

> **Proposition 1.5 (The kinship: contents are Darboux ledgers).** Let $A \subseteq [a,b]$ and let $\mathbf{1}_A$ be its indicator. Then
>
> $$\underline{c}(A) = \underline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_A \qquad\text{and}\qquad \overline{c}(A) = \overline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_A .$$
>
> In particular $A$ is Jordan measurable exactly when $\mathbf{1}_A$ is Riemann integrable, with content equal to integral. The rationals' failure below and the static's defeat (Volume One, Proposition 6.25 and Chapter 8) are one failure.

*Proof.* Lower ledgers. A partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ has $L(\mathbf{1}_A, P) = \sum' \Delta x_i$, the primed sum over slices lying *entirely* inside $A$ (the floor is one exactly there) — a finite disjoint family of intervals inside $A$, so $L(\mathbf{1}_A,P) \le \underline{c}(A)$. Conversely a finite disjoint packing of $A$ by intervals of total length $\ell$ yields, after listing all endpoints as a partition and shaving $\varepsilon$ at the joins (closed slices must sit inside $A$; open packing intervals lose two points' worth, which cost nothing after shaving), a lower sum exceeding $\ell - \varepsilon$. Suprema agree. The upper ledgers mirror: slices meeting $A$ versus finite covers, with the same endpoint bookkeeping. The desk leaves the mirrored half as drill within Problem I.4's ambit. ∎

> **Proposition 1.6 (Jordan's verdict on the rationals).** For $A = \Q \cap [0,1]$: $\underline{c}(A) = 0$ and $\overline{c}(A) = 1$. The set is not Jordan measurable.

*Proof.* Inner: an interval of positive length inside $A$ would consist of rationals only, impossible — the irrationals are dense (Volume One, Corollary 2.16). Only degenerate packings exist; the supremum is zero.

Outer: let $I_1, \dots, I_N$ be a finite cover of $A$ and let $F = \overline{I_1} \cup \cdots \cup \overline{I_N}$, the union of closures — a closed set of total length $\sum_j \lvert I_j \rvert$ at most (closing an interval adds endpoints, which carry no length). $F$ contains $A$, and $F$ is closed, so $F$ contains $\overline{A} = [0,1]$: the rationals are dense in the unit interval (Volume One, Theorem 2.15), and a closed superset of a set contains its closure. A finite union of intervals containing $[0,1]$ has total length at least $1$ (order the pieces meeting $[0,1]$ and walk from $0$ to $1$: each step is paid for by disjoint stretches of the pieces; the desk notes this is Jordan's own counting, or Volume One's Heine–Borel walk in miniature). Hence every finite cover totals at least $1$; the interval $[0,1]$ itself achieves $1$; the infimum is $1$. ∎

#### 1.4 The Outer Measure

> **Definition 1.7 ($(\circledast)$ Lebesgue outer measure — ring fifteen).** For *any* $A \subseteq \R$,
>
> $$m^{*}(A) \ =\ \inf \Bigl\{ \, \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \lvert I_k \rvert \ : \ A \subseteq \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} I_k, \ I_k \text{ intervals} \Bigr\},$$
>
> the infimum over all countable interval covers of the total length (a series of nonnegative terms: convergent or honestly infinite). Covers exist for every $A$ ($\R$ itself is a countable union of intervals), so the set of totals is a nonempty subset of $[0, \infty]$; if any total is finite, the set of finite totals is nonempty and bounded below by $0$, and *the bell rings — the fifteenth, the first of the volume*: the completeness axiom (Volume One, Axiom 2.6), and nothing else, delivers the greatest lower bound. (If every total is infinite, $m^{*}(A) = \infty$, an honest verdict.) The remaining suprema and infima of this chapter are clerical work upon this one and carry the standing annotation: completeness — small change, uncounted.

> **Remark 1.8 (Extended arithmetic; open covers at negligible cost).** Values live in $[0,\infty]$ with $a + \infty = \infty$; $\infty - \infty$ is never written. Two service facts, used silently hereafter. *Fattening:* any cover $\{I_k\}$ may be upgraded to *open* intervals $J_k \supseteq I_k$ with $\lvert J_k \rvert \le \lvert I_k \rvert + \varepsilon / 2^{k}$ — total cost at most $\varepsilon$, the geometric series footing the bill — so the infimum may be computed over open covers alone. *Degenerate intervals* (points) are permitted in covers and change nothing.

> **Proposition 1.9 (Monotonicity).** $A \subseteq B$ implies $m^{*}(A) \le m^{*}(B)$.

*Proof.* Every cover of $B$ covers $A$, so the infimum for $A$ runs over a larger family of candidate totals and cannot exceed the infimum for $B$. (With clause (i) of the contract: $m^{*}(\emptyset) = 0$, the empty set hiding under covers of arbitrarily small total.) ∎

> **Theorem 1.10 (The interval clause is kept).** For every interval $I$ with endpoints $a \le b$: $m^{*}(I) = b - a$.

*Proof.* ($\le$) $I \subseteq (a - \varepsilon, b + \varepsilon)$, a one-interval cover of total $b - a + 2\varepsilon$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$; the infimum dips below each, hence to $b - a$ at most.

($\ge$), the deep direction; it suffices to treat $I = [a,b]$ closed (any interval contains closed subintervals of length as near its own as desired, and monotonicity transfers the bound). Let $\{I_k\}$ be any countable cover of $[a,b]$; fatten to open $J_k$ at cost $\varepsilon$ (Remark 1.8). The open $J_k$ cover the compact $[a,b]$; Heine–Borel (Volume One, Theorem 5.18) extracts a finite committee $J_{k_1}, \dots, J_{k_N}$ still covering. Audit the committee by the walk: some member $(\alpha_1, \beta_1)$ contains $a$; if $\beta_1 > b$ stop; otherwise $\beta_1 \in [a,b]$ is covered by some member $(\alpha_2, \beta_2)$ with $\alpha_2 < \beta_1 < \beta_2$; continue. The walk visits distinct members with strictly increasing right endpoints, so it stops within $N$ steps, at some $\beta_M > b$. Then

$$\sum_{i=1}^{M} \lvert J_{(i)} \rvert \ \ge\ (\beta_1 - \alpha_1) + (\beta_2 - \beta_1) + \cdots + (\beta_M - \beta_{M-1}) \ =\ \beta_M - \alpha_1 \ >\ b - a,$$

each step's length at least the fresh ground gained (since $\alpha_{i+1} < \beta_i$). Hence $\sum_k \lvert I_k \rvert \ge \sum_k \lvert J_k \rvert - \varepsilon \ge b - a - \varepsilon$, for every cover and every $\varepsilon$; the infimum is at least $b - a$. — The clause cost compactness, exactly as narrated: the countable conspiracy collapses to an auditable committee, and Jordan's own counting convicts the committee. ∎

> **Theorem 1.11 (Countable subadditivity — the gambit's debut).** For any sets $A_1, A_2, A_3, \dots$
>
> $$m^{*} \Bigl( \bigcup_{k} A_k \Bigr) \ \le\ \sum_{k} m^{*}(A_k).$$

*Proof.* If any $m^{*}(A_k) = \infty$ the claim is vacuous. Otherwise let $\varepsilon > 0$. For each $k$, the infimum's approximation property (Volume One's oldest reflex) supplies a cover $\{I_{k,j}\}_j$ of $A_k$ with $\sum_j \lvert I_{k,j} \rvert \le m^{*}(A_k) + \varepsilon/2^{k}$. Pool the covers: $\{I_{k,j}\}_{k,j}$ is a countable family (a countable union of countable families — Volume One, Chapter 3's census) covering $\bigcup_k A_k$, of total

$$\sum_{k} \sum_{j} \lvert I_{k,j} \rvert \ \le\ \sum_k \Bigl( m^{*}(A_k) + \frac{\varepsilon}{2^k} \Bigr) \ =\ \sum_k m^{*}(A_k) + \varepsilon,$$

the geometric series picking up the bill. One cover within $\varepsilon$ of the target, for every $\varepsilon$: the infimum obeys. *The epsilon-over-two-to-the-k gambit, christened* — a fixed tolerance spent across countably many claimants; it recurs until the finale. ∎

> **Theorem 1.12 (Every countable set is null).** If $A \subseteq \R$ is countable, then $m^{*}(A) = 0$.

*Proof.* Enumerate $A = \{a_1, a_2, \dots\}$ (finite sets: pad the argument or stop early). Given $\varepsilon > 0$, house $a_k$ in an interval of length $\varepsilon / 2^{k}$ centred there. The family covers $A$ with total $\varepsilon$ exactly. So $m^{*}(A) \le \varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$, and $m^{*}(A) \ge 0$ always: $m^{*}(A) = 0$. In particular $m^{*}(\Q \cap [0,1]) = 0$ and $m^{*}(\Q) = 0$: the set that defeated Jordan is dispatched, and the entire difference is the word *countable*. ∎

> **Definition 1.13 (Measure zero).** $A \subseteq \R$ has *measure zero* (is *null*) when $m^{*}(A) = 0$: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are countably many intervals covering $A$ of total length below $\varepsilon$. This is the phrase Volume One's finale quoted as prophecy (Volume One, Chapter 8, the Lebesgue criterion, still on credit — proof at Chapter 4 of this volume); debt eleven pays its first instalment here.

> **Proposition 1.14 (The null family is a sigma-ideal).** (i) If $B \subseteq A$ and $A$ is null, $B$ is null. (ii) If each of $A_1, A_2, \dots$ is null, so is $\bigcup_k A_k$.

*Proof.* (i) is monotonicity (Proposition 1.9). (ii) is countable subadditivity (Theorem 1.11): $m^{*}(\bigcup A_k) \le \sum_k 0 = 0$. Hereditary downward, closed under countable assembly: negligibility with working papers. When "almost everywhere" arrives in force, these two laws discharge exceptional sets by the countable armful. ∎

> **Theorem 1.15 (The catch — stated on credit).** There is no assignment $\mu$ defined on *all* subsets of $\R$ satisfying the full contract of Definition 1.1 — nonnegativity with $\mu(\emptyset) = 0$, intervals to length, translation invariance, and countable additivity. In particular $m^{*}$, which keeps the first three clauses on all sets, is not countably additive on all sets.

*On credit.* The proof is the Vitali construction, Chapter 3's centrepiece, with the Axiom of Choice named in the indictment; nothing in this volume uses the catch before its trial. Until then it stands as the season's motivation: some sets must be turned away, and the honest question is which stay.

#### 1.5 Sigma-Algebras and the Borel Estate

> **Definition 1.16 (Algebra; sigma-algebra).** A collection $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of $\R$ (or of any ambient set) is a *sigma-algebra* when: (i) $\emptyset \in \mathcal{A}$; (ii) $A \in \mathcal{A}$ implies $A^{c} \in \mathcal{A}$; (iii) $A_1, A_2, \dots \in \mathcal{A}$ implies $\bigcup_k A_k \in \mathcal{A}$. Weakening (iii) to finite unions defines an *algebra*. Consequences, by De Morgan (Volume One, Chapter 1's toolkit): the ambient set belongs ($\emptyset^{c}$); countable intersections belong ($\bigcap A_k = (\bigcup A_k^{c})^{c}$); differences belong. The walls are drawn exactly where the traffic runs: complements and countable assemblies are what limiting arguments perform.

> **Remark 1.17 (Three specimens).** The tribe of two, $\{\emptyset, \R\}$: closed under everything, useless for everything. The all-subsets tribe $\mathcal{P}(\R)$: maximal hospitality, and the catch (Theorem 1.15) bars it from carrying the contract. The countable-or-co-countable tribe $\{A : A \text{ countable or } A^{c} \text{ countable}\}$: a genuine sigma-algebra containing every singleton yet not $[0, \tfrac12]$ — dissected in Problem II.1. Membership is a distinction.

> **Theorem 1.18 (Generated sigma-algebras exist — from above).** Let $\mathcal{G}$ be any collection of subsets. Among all sigma-algebras containing $\mathcal{G}$ there is a smallest, written $\sigma(\mathcal{G})$: it is contained in every sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal{G}$.

*Proof.* The family of sigma-algebras containing $\mathcal{G}$ is nonempty: $\mathcal{P}(\R)$ qualifies. Let $\sigma(\mathcal{G})$ be their intersection — the sets belonging to *every* sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal{G}$, the unanimous sets. The three closure checks, each one line: $\emptyset$ belongs to every chamber, hence unanimously. If $A$ is unanimous then, chamber by chamber, $A^{c}$ belongs (each chamber is a sigma-algebra), hence $A^{c}$ is unanimous. If $A_1, A_2, \dots$ are unanimous then each chamber contains them all and therefore their union: the union is unanimous. So $\sigma(\mathcal{G})$ is a sigma-algebra; it contains $\mathcal{G}$ (every chamber does); and it is contained in every containing sigma-algebra, being their intersection — unanimity cannot outvote a chamber. Floor-by-floor construction from below is not available at any countable stage (the Notes gesture at the transfinite abyss); the intersection from above is the whole trick. ∎

> **Definition 1.19 (The Borel estate).** $\mathcal{B} = \sigma(\{\text{open subsets of } \R\})$: the *Borel sets*. Every set this course has ever named in anger — intervals, opens, closeds, $\Q$, the irrationals, the dust, every continuity set — is Borel; producing a non-Borel set requires the ghost-machinery of Chapter 3 or deliberate transfinite bureaucracy (Notes).

> **Theorem 1.20 (The estate does not depend on the founder's taste).** $\sigma(\text{open sets}) = \sigma(\text{all intervals}) = \sigma(\text{open intervals}) = \sigma(\text{open intervals with rational endpoints})$.

*Proof.* Write $\mathcal{B}$, $\mathcal{I}$, $\mathcal{I}_{o}$, $\mathcal{I}_{\Q}$ for the four generated tribes; we chain inclusions both ways, using twice the master principle: if every member of $\mathcal{G}_1$ lies in $\sigma(\mathcal{G}_2)$, then $\sigma(\mathcal{G}_1) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{G}_2)$ — $\sigma(\mathcal{G}_2)$ is a sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal{G}_1$, and the smallest such is contained in it.

$\mathcal{I}_{\Q} \subseteq \mathcal{I}_{o} \subseteq \mathcal{I}$: generators nest. $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \mathcal{B}$: every interval is Borel — open intervals are open; $[a,b] = \bigcap_n (a - \tfrac1n,\, b + \tfrac1n)$, a countable intersection of opens; half-open likewise, one side at a time. $\mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{I}_{o}$: every open set is a countable disjoint union of open beads — Volume One's structure theorem (Proposition 5.3) — hence belongs to $\sigma(\text{open intervals})$, care of closure clause (iii); unbounded beads are countable unions of bounded ones. $\mathcal{I}_{o} \subseteq \mathcal{I}_{\Q}$: every open interval is a countable union of rational-endpoint ones — pick rational endpoints marching out to the true ones, density (Volume One, Theorem 2.15) supplying the recruits. The chain closes: all four tribes are one estate. The rational-endpoint generating set is *countable* — a fact of consequence for the season's bookkeeping and for Chapter 8's dictionary. ∎

> **Definition 1.21 (The ladder's first rungs).** A set is $F_{\sigma}$ when it is a countable union of closed sets; $G_{\delta}$ when a countable intersection of open sets. (F for *fermé*, sigma for sum; G for *Gebiet*, delta for *Durchschnitt*: the subject's bilingual fossils.) Complementation exchanges the two rungs, by De Morgan.

> **Proposition 1.22 (Rung calibrations).** (i) $\Q$ is $F_{\sigma}$; the irrationals are $G_{\delta}$. (ii) Every closed set is $F_{\sigma}$ and every open set $G_{\delta}$, trivially; moreover every open set is $F_{\sigma}$ and every closed set $G_{\delta}$.

*Proof.* (i) Singletons are closed; $\Q = \bigcup_{q \in \Q} \{q\}$ is a countable union of them. Complement and De Morgan deliver the irrationals as $G_{\delta}$. (ii) For open $U$: write $U$ as a countable union of open beads (Volume One, Proposition 5.3) and each bounded bead $(a,b)$ as $\bigcup_n [a + \tfrac1n,\, b - \tfrac1n]$ (fattened endpoints, run inward; unbounded beads as $\bigcup_n [a + \tfrac1n,\, n]$ and kin) — a countable union of closed sets. A countable union of countable unions is countable (Volume One, Chapter 3). Closed sets as $G_{\delta}$: complements. ∎

#### 1.6 The Continuity-Set Anatomy

> **Definition 1.23 (Oscillation).** For $f : \R \to \R$ (or on an interval), the *swing* on a set $W$ where $f$ is bounded is $\omega_f(W) = \sup_W f - \inf_W f$ (unbounded: $\omega_f(W) = \infty$). The *oscillation at a point* is
>
> $$\omega_f(x) \ =\ \inf_{\delta > 0} \, \omega_f\bigl( (x - \delta,\, x + \delta) \bigr),$$
>
> the swings settling downward as windows shrink (monotone in $\delta$; the infimum is small change, uncounted).

> **Lemma 1.24 (Continuity is oscillation zero).** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only if $\omega_f(x) = 0$.

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) Given $\varepsilon > 0$, continuity yields $\delta$ with $\lvert f(y) - f(x) \rvert < \varepsilon/2$ on the window, so the swing there is at most $\varepsilon$; the infimum dips below every $\varepsilon$. ($\Leftarrow$) If $\omega_f(x) = 0$: given $\varepsilon$, some window swings below $\varepsilon$; on it, $\lvert f(y) - f(x) \rvert \le \omega_f(W) < \varepsilon$ — both values live in the window's range. That is continuity's definition (Volume One, Chapter 6). ∎

> **Remark 1.25 (Calibrations).** The static (Volume One, Definition 6.24): every window contains rationals and irrationals (Volume One, 2.15–2.16), so every swing is $1$: $\omega_D \equiv 1$. Thomae (Volume One, Definition 6.26): at irrational $x$, oscillation zero (continuity, Volume One, Theorem 6.27); at rational $p/q$ in lowest terms, oscillation exactly $1/q$ — the value there is $1/q$, while nearby values are small (the counting lemma inside Volume One's Theorem 6.27 forces large denominators nearby) and irrationals nearby read zero, so the swing settles to the fraction's own loudness. The step function: oscillation equal to the jump's height at the jump, zero elsewhere. The cornered ramp (Volume One, Chapter 8): oscillation zero even at the corner — the gauge detects broken continuity, not broken smoothness.

> **Lemma 1.26 (The quiet sets are open).** For every $c > 0$, the set $V_c = \{ x : \omega_f(x) < c \}$ is open.

*Proof.* Let $x \in V_c$. The infimum's approximation property produces a witness window $W = (x - \delta, x + \delta)$ with $\omega_f(W) < c$. Every resident $y \in W$ owns a sub-window $W' \subseteq W$ centred at $y$ (openness of the interval), and swings only shrink on subsets: $\omega_f(W') \le \omega_f(W) < c$, so $\omega_f(y) < c$. Thus $W \subseteq V_c$: quietness certified by one window is inherited by everyone living in it, and $V_c$ contains a neighbourhood of each of its points — open, by the very definition (Volume One, Chapter 5). ∎

> **Theorem 1.27 (Every continuity set is a $G_{\delta}$).** For every $f$, the set $C_f$ of points of continuity satisfies
>
> $$C_f \ =\ \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} \, \Bigl\{ x : \omega_f(x) < \tfrac{1}{n} \Bigr\},$$
>
> a countable intersection of open sets.

*Proof.* By Lemma 1.24, $x \in C_f$ iff $\omega_f(x) = 0$ iff $\omega_f(x) < 1/n$ for every $n$ — a nonnegative quantity below every threshold is zero, the Archimedean gate (Volume One, Theorem 2.12). Each threshold set is open by Lemma 1.26. No hypothesis on $f$ was used: the theorem binds every function whatsoever. ∎

#### 1.7 The Refusal and the Ceremony

> **Theorem 1.28 (The rationals are not a $G_{\delta}$).** There do not exist open sets $G_1, G_2, \dots$ with $\Q = \bigcap_n G_n$.

*Proof.* Suppose otherwise. Each $G_n \supseteq \Q$ is open, and dense — it houses the dense tenant $\Q$ (Volume One, Theorem 2.15). For each rational $q$, the punctured line $\R \setminus \{q\}$ is open (a point is closed) and dense (no interval fits in a point). The family $\{G_n\}_n \cup \{\R \setminus \{q\}\}_{q \in \Q}$ is a countable family of open dense sets (countable plus countable, Volume One, Chapter 3). Its intersection is empty: a surviving point would be rational (unanimity of the $G_n$) yet avoid every rational (the punctures). But Baire's theorem (Volume One, Theorem 5.28, with its dense-intersection reading) makes any countable intersection of open dense subsets of $\R$ dense, hence nonempty. Contradiction; the supposition dies. Monsieur Baire's second and final engagement, discharged. ∎

> **Theorem 1.29 (The ceremony: debt nine paid).** There is no function $f : \R \to \R$ whose set of continuity points is exactly $\Q$.

*Proof.* $C_f$ is a $G_{\delta}$ (Theorem 1.27); $\Q$ is not (Theorem 1.28). Two lines, nine episodes in the arranging. ∎

> **Remark 1.30 (The census closes exactly).** Thomae's function realizes the irrationals as a continuity set (lawfully: they are $G_{\delta}$); the rationals are forbidden; and the characterization is complete in both directions: *every* $G_{\delta}$ subset of $\R$ is the continuity set of some function — Problem III.1, starred, the two-sign construction staged in hints. The continuity sets are precisely the $G_{\delta}$ sets; nothing else about a candidate set — cardinality, density, order — is relevant. Volume One's Episode Six inventory (everything; nothing; exactly the irrationals; never exactly the rationals) stands fully explained.

#### 1.8 Problems

##### Tier I — Calisthenics

1. **I.1** Directly from Definition 1.7: every finite set has outer measure zero. (Do not cite Theorem 1.12; build the cover.)
1. **I.2** For the displaced interval $[a,b] + t$: exhibit covers witnessing $m^{*}([a,b] + t) \le b - a$, and cite the theorem that forces equality once translation invariance (Problem II.3) is in hand.
1. **I.3** Nested pairs, worked: from the definitions alone, verify $m^{*}(\{0\}) \le m^{*}([0, \tfrac12]) \le m^{*}([0,1])$, then replace the middle term by its exact value.
1. **I.4** The two-set rehearsal for the gambit: given $m^{*}(A), m^{*}(B) < \infty$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, produce a single cover of $A \cup B$ of total below $m^{*}(A) + m^{*}(B) + \varepsilon$, splitting the tolerance in half. Then complete the mirrored half of Proposition 1.5 (upper ledgers), which uses the same endpoint bookkeeping.
1. **I.5** De Morgan drills: from Definition 1.16's three clauses, derive membership of the ambient set, of countable intersections, and of set differences, each in one line.
1. **I.6** Membership audits in the countable-or-co-countable tribe: the even integers; the rationals; $[0,1]$; the irrationals; a set containing exactly one point of each interval $[n, n+1)$. Verdicts with one-line warrants.
1. **I.7** Certify $[a, b)$ as both $F_{\sigma}$ and $G_{\delta}$, with explicit sequences of closed and open sets.
1. **I.8** Oscillation readings, with one-line justifications: the step function at and off its jump; the parabola everywhere; the static everywhere.

##### Tier II — The Real Thing

1. **II.1** (*The middle specimen.*) Prove the countable-or-co-countable collection is a sigma-algebra (the union clause splits by cases on whether some member is co-countable); show it contains every singleton but not $[0, \tfrac12]$; and identify it as $\sigma(\{\text{singletons}\})$ — the estate the points alone can afford.
1. **II.2** (*The engine's two faces.*) Let $\mu \ge 0$ on a sigma-algebra satisfy $\mu(\emptyset) = 0$ and finite additivity. Prove: $\mu$ is countably additive if and only if $\mu$ is continuous along swelling chains (Proposition 1.3(i)). Solved in full below, completing the crankshaft argument.
1. **II.3** (*Clause three for the new instrument.*) Prove $m^{*}(A + t) = m^{*}(A)$ for every $A$ and $t$: covers slide rigidly with their lengths in their luggage. Solved in full below.
1. **II.4** (*The refusal, generalized.*) Prove there is no countable *dense* $G_{\delta}$ subset of $\R$: Baire refires under your hand. Conclude anew that $\Q$ is not $G_{\delta}$, and locate exactly where density entered.
1. **II.5** (*The gauge's grain.*) Prove that for every $c > 0$, the set $\{ x : \omega_f(x) \ge c \}$ is closed; conclude the discontinuity set of any function is an $F_{\sigma}$. (The dual reading of Lemma 1.26; the discontinuity set's anatomy, dual to the continuity set's.)
1. **II.6** (*Thomae, certified twice.*) Certify that Thomae's continuity set — the irrationals — is $G_{\delta}$ two ways: by the anatomy (Theorem 1.27 applied to Thomae), and by direct exhibition of open sets intersecting to the irrationals. Verify the two exhibitions differ.

##### Tier III — For the Ambitious $\star$

1. **III.1** $\star$ (*The census closed: every $G_{\delta}$ is a continuity set.*) Let $G = \bigcap_n U_n$ with $U_n$ open; arrange $U_1 \supseteq U_2 \supseteq \cdots$ (intersect initial segments). For $x \notin G$ let $m(x)$ be the least $n$ with $x \notin U_n$ (well-ordering, Volume One, Chapter 1). Define $f = 0$ on $G$; $f(x) = 1/m(x)$ for $x \notin G$ rational; $f(x) = -1/m(x)$ for $x \notin G$ irrational. Prove $C_f = G$. Hints below; this is the two-sign construction the ceremony's closing remark invoked.
1. **III.2** $\star$ (*The ladder ascends.*) Prove the rationals are $F_{\sigma}$ but not $G_{\delta}$, and the irrationals $G_{\delta}$ but not $F_{\sigma}$; then show $A = (\Q \cap (-\infty, 0)) \cup ((\R \setminus \Q) \cap (0, \infty))$ is neither $F_{\sigma}$ nor $G_{\delta}$ — localize Baire on each half-line. References in the Notes for the ladder's transfinite continuation.
1. **III.3** $\star$ (*Jordan anatomized.*) Prove: a bounded set is Jordan measurable if and only if its topological boundary $\partial A$ has outer content zero — equivalently (for bounded sets, via Theorem 1.10's methods) measure zero. Test the criterion on the rationals of the unit interval ($\partial = [0,1]$) and on the dust (next chapter completes the verdict).

#### 1.9 Hints

**II.1.** For the union clause: if every $A_k$ is countable, the union is countable (Volume One, Chapter 3); if some $A_{k_0}$ is co-countable, the union's complement sits inside $A_{k_0}^{c}$. For $\sigma(\{\text{singletons}\})$: show the tribe is a sigma-algebra containing the singletons, and that any such sigma-algebra contains every countable set and every co-countable set.

**II.4.** Suppose $D = \{d_1, d_2, \dots\}$ countable, dense, and $= \bigcap_n G_n$ with $G_n$ open (dense, since $D$ is). The punctured lines $\R \setminus \{d_k\}$ are open; dense because a puncture cannot contain an interval. Intersect everything and apply Baire. Density of $D$ entered twice: making the $G_n$ dense, and making the contradiction bite ($\Q$ qualifies; a countable *closed* set need not).

**II.5.** The complement of $\{ \omega_f \ge c \}$ is $\bigcup_{c' < c} V_{c'}$ — or directly: $V_c$ open for every $c$ (Lemma 1.26) and $\{\omega_f \ge c\} = \R \setminus V_c$. For the $F_{\sigma}$ conclusion: the discontinuity set is $\bigcup_n \{ \omega_f \ge 1/n \}$.

**II.6.** Direct exhibition: the irrationals are $\bigcap_{q \in \Q} (\R \setminus \{q\})$, a countable intersection of opens. The anatomy's exhibition uses the quiet sets $V_{1/n}$ of Thomae's oscillation — compute which points each $V_{1/n}$ admits (rationals with denominator above $n$, and all irrationals), and observe the two families differ set by set though their intersections agree.

**III.1.** Continuity on $G$: for $x \in G$ and $N$ given, $W = \bigcap_{n \le N} U_n$ is an open neighbourhood of $x$; any $y \in W$ has either $f(y) = 0$ ($y \in G$) or $m(y) > N$, whence $\lvert f(y) \rvert < 1/N$. Discontinuity at $x \notin G$ with $m(x) = k$: every window at $x$ contains points of the opposite rationality class (Volume One, 2.15–2.16); such a point $y$ gives either $f(y) = 0$ (if $y \in G$: gap $1/k$) or $f(y)$ of opposite sign (gap exceeding $1/k$). Either way $\omega_f(x) \ge 1/k > 0$. Mind that $m$ is well-defined only off $G$, and that the decreasing arrangement of the $U_n$ is what makes $m(y) > N$ mean $y \in U_1, \dots, U_N$.

**III.2.** If the irrationals were $F_{\sigma}$, the rationals would be $G_{\delta}$ (De Morgan): Theorem 1.28 forbids. For $A$: were $A$ $G_{\delta}$, then $A \cap (-\infty, 0) = \Q \cap (-\infty, 0)$ would be $G_{\delta}$ in the open half-line, and Baire localizes to any complete-metric-flavoured stage — run the punctured-lines argument inside $(-\infty, 0)$; the mirrored half kills $F_{\sigma}$. References: Oxtoby for the honest treatment of relative Baire arguments.

**III.3.** Key identity: for bounded $A$, $\overline{c}(A) = \overline{c}(\overline{A})$ (closing a finite cover costs endpoints only) and $\underline{c}(A) = \underline{c}(A^{\circ})$ (an interval inside $A$ avoids the boundary after shaving). Then $\overline{c}(A) - \underline{c}(A) = \overline{c}(\partial A)$ via $\overline{A} = A^{\circ} \sqcup \partial A$ and finite additivity of content on such splittings.

#### 1.10 Solutions

**Tier I (terse).** **I.1** House the $j$-th of the $N$ points in an interval of length $\varepsilon / N$: total $\varepsilon$, for every $\varepsilon$; the infimum is $0$. **I.2** $[a,b] + t = [a+t, b+t]$, an interval of the same length; the cover $(a + t - \varepsilon, b + t + \varepsilon)$ witnesses $\le b - a + 2\varepsilon$; Theorem 1.10 forces $= b - a$ (or II.3 plus the theorem, as the drill anticipates). **I.3** Monotonicity twice (Proposition 1.9); middle term $= \tfrac12$ by Theorem 1.10. **I.4** Covers within $\varepsilon/2$ of each outer measure pool to a countable cover of the union (two countables); total below the sum plus $\varepsilon$. Mirrored ledgers: slices of a partition meeting $A$ form a finite cover of $A$; conversely a finite cover's endpoints, listed as a partition with $\varepsilon$-shaving at the joins, give an upper sum within $\varepsilon$ of the cover's total. **I.5** Ambient set $= \emptyset^{c}$; intersections by $\bigcap A_k = \bigl( \bigcup A_k^{c} \bigr)^{c}$; difference $A \setminus B = A \cap B^{c}$. **I.6** Evens: countable, in. Rationals: countable, in. $[0,1]$: uncountable with uncountable complement, out. Irrationals: complement countable, in. The transversal of the intervals $[n, n+1)$: countably infinite (one point per integer), in — the tribe cares only for cardinality, not location. **I.7** $[a,b) = \bigcup_n [a,\, b - \tfrac{b-a}{n}]$ (closed) $= \bigcap_n (a - \tfrac1n,\, b)$ (open). **I.8** Step: at the jump every window swings the jump's height $h$, and constancy elsewhere swings nought — $\omega = h$ at the jump, $0$ off it. Parabola: continuous everywhere (Volume One, Chapter 6), so $\omega \equiv 0$ (Lemma 1.24). Static: every window contains both values $0$ and $1$ (density both ways): $\omega \equiv 1$.

**II.2 (solution in full).** ($\Rightarrow$) is Proposition 1.3(i). ($\Leftarrow$) Let $E_1, E_2, \dots$ be pairwise disjoint members with union $E$. The partial unions $U_n = \bigcup_{k \le n} E_k$ form a swelling chain in the sigma-algebra with union $E$, so continuity gives $\mu(E) = \lim_n \mu(U_n)$. Finite additivity prices each stage: $\mu(U_n) = \sum_{k \le n} \mu(E_k)$, a partial sum. The limit of the partial sums *is* the series (nonnegative terms; Volume One, Chapter 4's monotone license makes the limit exist in $[0,\infty]$): $\mu(E) = \sum_{k} \mu(E_k)$. Countable additivity holds; the engine and the clause are one mechanism seen from two sides, as the episode claimed.

**II.3 (solution in full).** Fix $A$ and $t$. If $\{I_k\}$ covers $A$, then $\{I_k + t\}$ covers $A + t$ — $a \in A$ gives $a \in I_k$ for some $k$, so $a + t \in I_k + t$ — and translated intervals keep their lengths: $\lvert I_k + t \rvert = \lvert I_k \rvert$ (endpoints shift together). So every candidate total for $A$ is a candidate total for $A + t$: $m^{*}(A + t) \le m^{*}(A)$, the infimum running over a family at least as rich. Apply the same inequality to the set $A + t$ and the shift $-t$: $m^{*}(A) = m^{*}((A + t) + (-t)) \le m^{*}(A + t)$. The two inequalities close: $m^{*}(A + t) = m^{*}(A)$. Clause three of the contract is kept by the new instrument — the clause that will sign Chapter 3's confession is, for now, in impeccable standing.

#### 1.11 Notes

*History.* Jordan's content reached its mature form in the second edition of his *Cours d'analyse* (1893), building on Peano; it is the exact set-theoretic shadow of Riemann's integral, as Proposition 1.5 makes precise. Borel introduced countably additive measure on the sets his operations generate in *Leçons sur la théorie des fonctions* (1898) — the estate bears his name by right. Lebesgue's thesis, *Intégrale, longueur, aire* (Annali di Matematica, 1902), contains the outer measure, the measurable sets, and most of this season in embryo; Lebesgue was indeed teaching at the lycée of Nancy as he wrote it. Vitali's construction (1905) waits at Chapter 3. Baire's theorem is from his own thesis (1899). The characterization of continuity sets — necessity tonight, the converse in Problem III.1 — goes back to W. H. Young (1903) and is treated in Hahn's *Theorie der reellen Funktionen*; our two-sign construction is the standard modern staging.

*The ladder above the first rungs.* $F_{\sigma\delta}$, $G_{\delta\sigma}$, and onward: the Borel hierarchy genuinely ascends through all countable transfinite stages — no countable list of operations exhausts $\mathcal{B}$ — and its honest treatment needs ordinals. Oxtoby, *Measure and Category*, chapters 1–3, is the season's recommended companion for exactly this circle of ideas (Baire, hierarchy, the category/measure duality previewed next chapter); Kechris, *Classical Descriptive Set Theory*, for the abyss in full.

*Reading.* Axler, *Measure, Integration & Real Analysis* (the season's companion, per the plan's shelf: chapter 2A covers tonight's ground); Royden–Fitzpatrick, chapters 1–2; Folland, chapter 1; Stein–Shakarchi, *Real Analysis*, chapter 1. Tao's *An Introduction to Measure Theory* opens with a beautiful extended meditation on exactly tonight's contract-and-catch dialectic.

*Forward pointers.* The scorecard's unpaid half — countable additivity on a tribe — is Chapter 2 (Carathéodory); the catch's trial, Chapter 3 (Vitali, Choice, Banach–Tarski); the null ideal meets "almost everywhere" in force at Chapter 4, where the static is tamed and Volume One's criterion is finally proved.

#### Episode Digest

**The argument of the hour.** One strange sentence selects the tribe. A set is measurable when it splits every test set cleanly — the good citizen, the honest knife, the balanced audit — and the criterion's entire content is the reverse of subadditivity: no phantom mass at the cut. Null sets pass (completeness in embryo); half-lines pass (the turnstile to geometry); and Carathéodory's theorem builds the rest by a four-step staircase — symmetry (complements free), composition (honest knives compound), proportion (disjoint knives cut every cake in exact proportion, by induction), limit (the monotone license closes both the sigma-algebra walls and countable additivity). On the tribe, Episode One's contract holds entire — and uniquely: nothing else was ever on offer. The machine then runs: open sets by beads; the irrationals of the unit interval at measure one; the dust — uncountable, the size of the continuum — at measure **zero**, the account three episodes and two seasons old, paid in four sentences; the fat dust (Smith–Volterra–Cantor) at measure one half though nowhere dense, divorcing category's smallness from measure's; the stacked fat dusts, meagre yet of full measure, and their complement, residual yet null — never say small without naming the judge. Jordan's regime is absorbed intact; the construction is dimension-blind (area, volume: same theorems verbatim); and the commonwealth outnumbers the Borel estate two-to-the-continuum to continuum, yet every citizen is a G-delta shaved of a null set: the vastness is veil, the substance Borel.
