| [2pt] "almost everywhere" | a.e.: off a null set | Prop. 4.16 |
| [2pt] "the devil's staircase" | $c : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ | Thm. 4.21 |

*Extended values.* Functions take values in $[-\infty, \infty]$; $\{f = \infty\} = \bigcap_n \{f > n\}$ is a citizen; the arithmetic conventions of Chapter 1 (one prohibition) govern, with $0 \cdot \infty = 0$ in the merchant's multiplication — the convention that makes weightless ground carry any value for free, and the taming one line.

#### 4.2 Measurable Functions

> **Definition 4.1 (Measurable function).** Let $E \in \mathcal{M}$. A function $f : E \to [-\infty, \infty]$ is *measurable* when $\{ f > a \} = \{ x \in E : f(x) > a \}$ is a citizen for every $a \in \R$.

> **Proposition 4.2 (Equivalent thresholds; Borel preimages).** For $f : E \to [-\infty, \infty]$ the following are equivalent: $\{f > a\} \in \mathcal{M}$ for all $a$; $\{f \ge a\} \in \mathcal{M}$ for all $a$; $\{f < a\} \in \mathcal{M}$ for all $a$; $\{f \le a\} \in \mathcal{M}$ for all $a$. Any of them implies $f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{M}$ for every Borel $B \subseteq \R$.

*Proof.* $\{f \ge a\} = \bigcap_n \{f > a - \tfrac1n\}$ and $\{f > a\} = \bigcup_n \{f \ge a + \tfrac1n\}$: countable tribe operations convert the two strict/weak forms; complements within $E$ convert to the two below-forms. For Borel preimages: the collection $\{ B : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{M} \}$ is a sigma-algebra (preimages respect complements and unions), and it contains the half-lines, hence the intervals, hence — the estate's robustness, Chapter 1, Theorem 1.20 — all of $\mathcal{B}$. ∎

> **Proposition 4.3 (The parade).** Continuous functions on citizens are measurable ($\{f > a\}$ is the trace of an open set); monotone functions (the pile above a waterline is an interval or half-line trace); step and simple functions; indicators of citizens; the static and Thomae's function; and any function on a null ground. Ghost indicators ($\mathbf{1}_{V}$, $V$ Vitali's delegation) are the canonical non-measurable specimens.

*Proof.* Each is a one-line pile audit; the desk records the static's: $\{D > a\}$ is $\emptyset$ ($a \ge 1$), $\Q \cap E$ ($0 \le a < 1$), or $E$ ($a < 0$) — citizens all. Problem I.1 drills the rest. ∎

> **Proposition 4.4 (The algebra).** If $f, g$ are measurable (finite-valued where combined) and $c \in \R$: $cf$, $f + g$, $fg$, $\lvert f \rvert$, $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$ are measurable.

*Proof.* The sum, the one with an idea: $f + g > a$ iff some rational $q$ has $f > q$ and $g > a - q$ (density splits the surplus), so $\{f + g > a\} = \bigcup_{q \in \Q} \bigl( \{f > q\} \cap \{g > a - q\} \bigr)$ — a countable union of citizens; the picket fence's contract, executed at the function level. Products via $fg = \tfrac14 \bigl( (f+g)^2 - (f-g)^2 \bigr)$ once squares are settled ($\{f^2 > a\}$ unwinds to two piles); moduli and max/min are unions and intersections of piles. Problem I.1's second half. ∎

> **Proposition 4.5 (Composition: the safe direction).** If $f$ is measurable and $g : \R \to \R$ is Borel measurable (in particular continuous), then $g \circ f$ is measurable. The reverse composition — a measurable function of a continuous function — can fail: Theorem 4.22.

*Proof.* $(g \circ f)^{-1}(a, \infty) = f^{-1}\bigl( g^{-1}(a,\infty) \bigr)$: $g^{-1}(a, \infty)$ is Borel, and Proposition 4.2 finishes. ∎

> **Theorem 4.6 (Limit stability — the crown of the class).** Let $f_1, f_2, \dots$ be measurable on $E$. Then $\sup_n f_n$, $\inf_n f_n$, $\limsup_n f_n$, $\liminf_n f_n$ are measurable; and if $f_n \to f$ pointwise on $E$, then $f$ is measurable.

*Proof.* $\{\sup_n f_n > a\} = \bigcup_n \{f_n > a\}$: some function clears the waterline — a countable union of citizens. Infima by $\inf f_n = -\sup(-f_n)$ (or the mirrored intersection). $\limsup_n f_n = \inf_{n} \sup_{k \ge n} f_k$: countable operations stacked twice, each stage measurable by the preceding clauses. Pointwise limits equal their limsup. No hypothesis beyond measurability was used; the sigma-algebra's countable clause is what every line spent. ∎

#### 4.3 Atoms, Staircases, and the Integral

> **Definition 4.7 (Simple functions; the merchant's multiplication).** $\varphi$ is *simple* when it takes finitely many values, each on a citizen: $\varphi = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \mathbf{1}_{A_i}$ with $A_i \in \mathcal{M}$ disjoint. For simple $\varphi \ge 0$,
>
> $$\int \varphi \, dm \ =\ \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \, m(A_i) \qquad (0 \cdot \infty = 0).$$

> **Proposition 4.8 (Well-priced; simple linearity and monotonicity).** The price is independent of the representation; for simple $\varphi, \psi \ge 0$ and $c \ge 0$: $\int (\varphi + \psi) = \int \varphi + \int \psi$, $\int c\varphi = c \int \varphi$, and $\varphi \le \psi \Rightarrow \int \varphi \le \int \psi$.

*Proof.* Two representations refine to a common one (intersect the storeys — Chapter 1's finite tribe operations), on which both prices telescope to the same sum; additivity of $m$ on the disjoint refinement is the only fact used. Linearity and monotonicity read off the common refinement likewise. (Problem I.2 drills a two-representation specimen.) ∎

> **Theorem 4.9 (The staircase of the range).** Let $f : E \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable. Define
>
> $$\varphi_n \ =\ \sum_{k=1}^{n 2^{n}} \frac{k-1}{2^{n}} \, \mathbf{1}_{A_{n,k}} \; + \; n \, \mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge n\}}, \qquad A_{n,k} = \Bigl\{ \tfrac{k-1}{2^n} \le f < \tfrac{k}{2^n} \Bigr\}.$$
>
> Each $\varphi_n$ is simple; $\varphi_n \le \varphi_{n+1} \le f$; and $\varphi_n \to f$ pointwise on $E$ — uniformly on any set where $f$ is bounded.

*Proof.* The bins $A_{n,k}$ are differences of piles: citizens (Proposition 4.2); finitely many storeys: simple. Monotonicity: passing $n \to n+1$ halves each denomination — a point binned at $\tfrac{k-1}{2^n}$ is re-binned at $\tfrac{2k-2}{2^{n+1}}$ or $\tfrac{2k-1}{2^{n+1}}$, never lower — and raises the ceiling. Convergence: if $f(x) < \infty$, then for $n > f(x)$ the assignment sits within $2^{-n}$ of $f(x)$; if $f(x) = \infty$, the assignments are $n \uparrow \infty$. Where $f \le K$: for $n > K$ the error is uniformly under $2^{-n}$. ∎

> **Definition 4.10 ($(\circledast)$ The integral — ring sixteen).** For measurable $f : E \to [0, \infty]$,
>
> $$\int_{E} f \, dm \ =\ \sup \Bigl\{ \int \varphi \, dm \ : \ 0 \le \varphi \le f, \ \varphi \text{ simple} \Bigr\} .$$
>
> *The bell rings — the sixteenth*: the supremum over the inventory of under-staircases exists in $[0, \infty]$ by the completeness axiom (finite case) and honest convention (infinite), the same authority that manufactured the Darboux ledgers at rings thirteen and fourteen. One ledger only, by design: measurability has done the vetting Riemann's upper book performed by hand (the bounded estate's Proposition 4.14 exhibits the second book collapsing onto the first where both exist), and Theorem 4.9 guarantees the supremum is *climbed*, not merely bounded. Nothing is refused; the value $\infty$ is an honest verdict.

> **Remark 4.11 (The handshake: the identity, re-integrated).** For $f(x) = x$ on $[0,1]$, the staircase $\varphi_n$ of Theorem 4.9 has bins $A_{n,k} = [\tfrac{k-1}{2^n}, \tfrac{k}{2^n})$ of measure $2^{-n}$, so
>
> $$\int \varphi_n \ =\ \sum_{k=1}^{2^{n}} \frac{k-1}{2^{n}} \cdot \frac{1}{2^{n}} \ =\ \frac{1}{4^{n}} \cdot \frac{2^{n}(2^{n}-1)}{2} \ =\ \frac12 - \frac{1}{2^{n+1}} \ \uparrow\ \frac12 ,$$
>
> and no under-staircase exceeds $\tfrac12$ (each is dominated by the Riemann upper ledger, or directly: Problem I.3). The new integral returns the schoolroom's one half; the general agreement is Theorem 4.19.

> **Definition 4.12 (Integrable; the general integral).** For measurable $f$: $f^{\pm} = \max(\pm f, 0)$ are measurable (Proposition 4.4), $f = f^{+} - f^{-}$, $\lvert f \rvert = f^{+} + f^{-}$. $f$ is *integrable* when $\int \lvert f \rvert \, dm < \infty$ (equivalently both $\int f^{\pm} < \infty$), and then $\int f \, dm = \int f^{+} - \int f^{-}$ — lawful subtraction. If exactly one part is infinite the integral is $\pm\infty$; if both, undefined.

> **Proposition 4.13 (Manners within tonight's reach).** (i) Monotonicity: $0 \le f \le g$ measurable $\Rightarrow \int f \le \int g$ (every under-staircase of $f$ under-staircases $g$). (ii) $\int c f = c \int f$ for $c \ge 0$ (staircases scale). (iii) Ground conventions: $\int_E f = \int f \mathbf{1}_E$, the two definitions agreeing storey by storey. (iv) $f = 0$ a.e. $\Rightarrow \int f = 0$ (every under-staircase's storeys of positive value stand on null ground). (v) **Bounded additivity**: for bounded measurable $f, g$ on finite-measure ground, $\int (f + g) = \int f + \int g$ — via Proposition 4.14's sandwiches (Problem II.2's ambit).

> **Proposition 4.14 (The bounded estate: two ledgers meet).** Let $f$ be measurable and bounded on $E$ with $m(E) < \infty$. Then
>
> $$\sup_{\substack{\varphi \le f \\ \varphi \text{ simple}}} \int \varphi \ =\ \inf_{\substack{\psi \ge f \\ \psi \text{ simple}}} \int \psi .$$

*Proof.* The staircase construction at resolution $n$ (ceiling above the bound) yields $\varphi_n \le f \le \varphi_n + 2^{-n}$ pointwise, so $\psi_n = \varphi_n + 2^{-n}$ over-staircases $f$ with $\int \psi_n - \int \varphi_n = 2^{-n} m(E) \to 0$; the sup and inf are pinched together. (Solved in full as Problem II.2, with the bounded-additivity dividend; the converse — ledger agreement forces measurability — is the desk's note for the ambitious, references supplied.) ∎

> **Remark 4.15 (The additivity credit — one week's maturity).** For arbitrary measurable $f, g \ge 0$, $\int (f+g) = \int f + \int g$: the $\ge$ direction is free (under-staircases add), and the $\le$ direction is **stated on credit tonight**, discharged in Chapter 5 as the monotone convergence theorem's first corollary (staircases $\varphi_n \uparrow f$, $\psi_n \uparrow g$ give $\varphi_n + \psi_n \uparrow f + g$; MCT passes the limit). No argument of this chapter uses the credit: the taming, the absorption, and the criterion live in the bounded estate, where Proposition 4.14 pays cash.

> **Proposition 4.16 (Almost everywhere, at work).** (i) If $f = g$ a.e. on $E$ and both are measurable, then $\int_E f = \int_E g$ (whenever either side is defined). (ii) If $f$ is measurable and $g = f$ a.e., then $g$ is measurable — completeness of $\mathcal{M}$ earning its keep.

*Proof.* (ii) $\{g > a\}$ differs from the citizen $\{f > a\}$ within the null disagreement set; the amnesty (Chapter 2, completeness) makes the difference a citizen, and the tribe's algebra reassembles. (i) For $f, g \ge 0$: any under-staircase of $f$ converts to one of $g$ by zeroing its storeys on the null disagreement — prices unchanged, $0 \cdot \infty = 0$ and Proposition 4.13(iv) covering the leftovers; the suprema agree. General case: positive and negative parts disagree only on the null set. ∎

> **Theorem 4.17 (The taming of the static — debt four, act three).** $\displaystyle \int_{[0,1]} D \, dm = 0$.

*Proof.* $D = 1 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\Q \cap [0,1]} + 0 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{[0,1] \setminus \Q}$ is simple; $\int D = 1 \cdot m(\Q \cap [0,1]) = 1 \cdot 0 = 0$. One line, as promised in Volume One, Chapter 8. *The three-act contract — born at Volume One's Definition 6.24, victorious over Riemann in Volume One, Chapter 8, tamed here — is complete.* ∎

#### 4.4 The Old Regime, Absorbed

> **Remark 4.18 (The boundary post: improper integrals).** The absorption below covers the *proper* Riemann integral. A conditionally convergent improper integral — finite by cancellation between infinite gains and infinite losses — has $\int \lvert f \rvert = \infty$ and is refused by Definition 4.12, on the same grounds Volume One's rearrangement theorem convicted conditional series: totals that depend on the order of summation have no order-free value, and the sorted count is order-free by construction. Standard specimen: the sign-alternating bump train with masses $1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots$ — improperly convergent to the alternating harmonic total, Lebesgue-undefined. Absolutely convergent improper integrals are absorbed (Problem III.2's ambit, via next week's tools). Lebesgue honours everything Riemann *proved*; some things Riemann merely got away with.

> **Theorem 4.19 (Riemann absorbed).** Let $f$ be (properly) Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$. Then $f$ is measurable, integrable, and $\int_{[a,b]} f \, dm = \text{(R)}\!\int_a^b f$.

*Proof.* $f$ is bounded (Riemann's ticket, Volume One). Take partitions $P_n$, each refining the last, mesh $\to 0$, with Darboux ledgers $L(f, P_n) \uparrow$ and $U(f, P_n) \downarrow$ toward the common Riemann value $R$ (integrability). Let $\varphi_n \le f \le \psi_n$ be the step functions taking the slice-infima and slice-suprema on $P_n$'s slices: simple functions with $\int \varphi_n = L(f, P_n)$ and $\int \psi_n = U(f, P_n)$ — the merchant's multiplication reading Darboux's books aloud. Refinement makes $\varphi_n \uparrow \varphi$ and $\psi_n \downarrow \psi$ pointwise (monotone bounded sequences; Volume One's license), with $\varphi \le f \le \psi$; both limits are measurable (Theorem 4.6). On the finite-measure frame, the bounded estate prices

$$\int (\psi - \varphi) \ \le\ \int (\psi_n - \varphi_n) \ =\ U(f, P_n) - L(f, P_n) \ \longrightarrow\ 0$$

(monotonicity; bounded additivity for the differences, Proposition 4.13(v)); so $\int (\psi - \varphi) = 0$ with $\psi - \varphi \ge 0$, forcing $\psi = \varphi$ a.e. (Problem I.6's little lemma: a nonnegative function of zero integral vanishes a.e.). Then $f$, trapped between a.e.-equal measurable functions, equals $\varphi$ a.e.: measurable by amnesty (Proposition 4.16(ii)), and

$$\int f \ =\ \int \varphi \ =\ \lim_n \int \varphi_n \ =\ \lim_n L(f, P_n) \ =\ R$$

(the middle equality by the bounded two-ledger pinch against $\psi_n$; partition endpoints, countably many, are null and filed). ∎

#### 4.5 The Prophecy, Proved

> **Theorem 4.20 (Lebesgue's criterion — debt ten retired).** Let $f$ be bounded on $[a,b]$, $\Delta_f$ its set of discontinuity points. Then $f$ is Riemann integrable if and only if $m(\Delta_f) = 0$.

*Proof.* Write $D_\sigma = \{ x : \omega_f(x) \ge \sigma \}$ (the loud sets; oscillation as in Chapter 1), so $\Delta_f = \bigcup_n D_{1/n}$ (Chapter 1's Lemma 1.24). Let $K$ bound $\lvert f \rvert$.

($\Rightarrow$) Fix $\sigma > 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Choose a partition with $U - L < \sigma \varepsilon$. On any slice whose *interior* meets $D_\sigma$, the slice's swing is at least $\sigma$ (the gauge reads a swing of at least $\sigma$ in every window of an interior loud point); letting $w$ be those slices' total width,

$$\sigma \varepsilon \ >\ U - L \ =\ \sum_i (\text{swing}_i)\, \Delta x_i \ \ge\ \sigma \, w,$$

so $w < \varepsilon$: the interior-loud slices cover $D_\sigma$ save the finitely many partition points, null. Hence $m^{*}(D_\sigma) < \varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon$: $D_\sigma$ is null, and $\Delta_f$ is a countable union of nulls — null (Chapter 1's ideal).

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $m(\Delta_f) = 0$; fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and set $\sigma = \varepsilon / \bigl( 2 (b - a) \bigr)$. The loud set $D_\sigma$ is closed (Chapter 1, Problem II.5's grain — proved there), bounded: compact; null (inside $\Delta_f$); so finitely many open intervals cover it with total length below $\varepsilon / (8K)$ (null + compact: a countable $\varepsilon$-cover admits a finite subcover). Off those intervals, the leftover $F$ is compact with every point quiet below $\sigma$: each $x \in F$ owns $\delta_x > 0$ with the window $(x - \delta_x, x + \delta_x)$ swinging under $\sigma$ (the gauge's approximation property); the half-radius windows cover $F$; extract a finite subcover (Heine–Borel, Volume One, Theorem 5.18 — the same manoeuvre as Heine–Cantor's proof, Volume One 6.22, and the kinship is the point); let $\delta$ be the least half-radius. Now partition $[a, b]$ by: the cover intervals' endpoints, and a mesh finer than $\delta$ elsewhere. Slices inside the loud cover: total width below $\varepsilon / (8K)$, swing at most $2K$ — contribution below $\varepsilon / 4$. Slices meeting $F$: each lies inside some full window (mesh under the half-radius), swing at most $\sigma$ — contribution at most $\sigma (b - a) = \varepsilon / 2$. Hence $U - L < \varepsilon$; the auditor's criterion (Volume One, Chapter 8) stamps. *The Volume One finale's prophecy stands proved; the vocabulary crisis is dissolved; the exhibits table reads as theorems, line by line.* ∎

#### 4.6 The Devil's Staircase

> **Theorem 4.21 (The Cantor function — debt eight's account closes).** There is a function $c : [0,1] \to [0,1]$, continuous and nondecreasing, with $c(0) = 0$, $c(1) = 1$, constant on each interval removed in the dust's construction — hence differentiable with $c' = 0$ at almost every point — and $\int_{[0,1]} c \, dm = \tfrac12$. Its entire unit of ascent is accomplished on the null dust.

*Proof.* *Construction.* Assign to the stage-$n$ removed middles, read left to right, the values $\tfrac{1}{2^n}, \tfrac{3}{2^n}, \dots, \tfrac{2^n - 1}{2^n}$ (each middle the dyadic mean of its neighbours' values); the assignments are consistent under staging and monotone across the complement. For $x \in C$ set $c(x) = \sup \{ c(t) : t \text{ in removed middles}, t \le x \}$ (sup over a nonempty bounded set — small change), with $c(0) = 0$; monotonicity extends.

*Continuity.* $c$ is monotone with range dense in $[0,1]$ — every dyadic value is attained on a middle. A monotone function's only discontinuities are jumps, and a jump omits an interval of values, contradicting dense range. So $c$ is continuous (and $c(1) = 1$ by the sup over values climbing to one).

*Flatness a.e.* On each removed middle $c$ is constant, so $c' = 0$ there; the middles carry measure one (Chapter 2); the dust where ascent happens is null.

*The integral.* The construction is symmetric under $x \mapsto 1 - x$ with values reflecting through $\tfrac12$: $c(x) + c(1 - x) = 1$ for all $x$ (verified on middles, extended by continuity). Reflection invariance of $m$ (Chapter 3, Problem I.7) gives $\int c(1 - x) \, dm = \int c \, dm$, so $2 \int c = \int \bigl( c(x) + c(1-x) \bigr) \, dm = m([0,1]) = 1$ (bounded additivity), and $\int c = \tfrac12$. ∎

> **Theorem 4.22 (The two gifts).** Let $h(x) = x + c(x)$ on $[0,1]$. Then $h$ is a homeomorphism onto $[0, 2]$ with $m\bigl( h(C) \bigr) = 1$; and there exist
>
> 1. **(i)** a measurable set $A \subseteq C$ (null, hence a citizen) that is *not Borel*;
> 1. **(ii)** a measurable function $g$ and a continuous function $F$ with $g \circ F$ non-measurable — the composition caution, detonated.
>
> (One conjuring, declared: the ghost inside $h(C)$ is Chapter 3's.)

*Proof.* $h$ is continuous and strictly increasing (identity strictly, $c$ nondecreasing): a continuous bijection $[0,1] \to [0,2]$, hence a homeomorphism (compact domain; Volume One's machinery). On each removed middle, $c$ is constant, so $h$ is a translation there: lengths preserved; the complement's beads carry total measure one into $[0,2]$, and additivity leaves $m(h(C)) = 2 - 1 = 1$. The ghost factory (Chapter 3, Theorem 3.6) supplies non-measurable $N \subseteq h(C)$. Set $A = h^{-1}(N) \subseteq C$: null by heredity, hence a citizen by amnesty. *Not Borel:* were $A$ Borel, then $N = (h^{-1})^{-1}(A)$ would be a Borel set's preimage under the continuous $h^{-1}$ — Borel (Proposition 4.2) — but ghosts are not even measurable. *The detonation:* $g = \mathbf{1}_{A}$ is measurable (citizen indicator); $F = h^{-1} : [0,2] \to [0,1]$ is continuous; and $g \circ F = \mathbf{1}_{N}$, whose unit pile is the ghost: non-measurable. *The veil made specimen: Chapter 2's count argued that non-Borel citizens exist; here is one, a single conjuring back.* ∎

#### 4.9 Solutions

**Tier I (terse).** **I.1**–**I.5** As drilled; I.4's verdicts: integrable; not integrable ($\int_0^1 1/x = \infty$: staircases $\sum 2^k \mathbf{1}$-flavoured climb unboundedly); integrable (mass one); integrable (bounded on finite ground); the bump train with masses $\tfrac1n$: refused, per the boundary post. **I.6** $\tfrac1n m(\{f \ge \tfrac1n\}) \le \int f = 0$ forces each pile null; their union is $\{f > 0\}$. **I.7** Thomae: simple it is not, but $t = 0$ a.e. (defects on $\Q$), so $\int t = 0$ by Proposition 4.16(i) against the zero function. **I.8** Ramp's step: Darboux $\tfrac12$ (Volume One); merchant: $0 \cdot \tfrac12 + 1 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac12$.

**II.2 (solution in full).** *The pinch.* With $K$ a bound and resolution $n > K$: Theorem 4.9's $\varphi_n$ has $f - 2^{-n} < \varphi_n \le f$ pointwise (the bin width), so $\psi_n = \varphi_n + 2^{-n} \mathbf{1}_E$ is simple with $f \le \psi_n$ and $\int \psi_n - \int \varphi_n = 2^{-n} m(E)$. Hence $\inf_{\psi \ge f} \int \psi - \sup_{\varphi \le f} \int \varphi \le 2^{-n} m(E) \to 0$; the reverse inequality is monotonicity (any $\varphi \le f \le \psi$ has $\int \varphi \le \int \psi$ via Proposition 4.8). *Bounded additivity.* For bounded $f, g \ge 0$ on finite ground: take under-staircases $\varphi \le f$, $\chi \le g$; $\varphi + \chi \le f + g$ is simple, so $\int f + \int g \le \int (f+g)$ (sup over sums). For $\le$: over-staircases $\psi \ge f$, $\omega \ge g$ give the simple $\psi + \omega \ge f + g$, whence every under-staircase of $f + g$ prices at most $\int \psi + \int \omega$ (Proposition 4.8); infimize using the pinch on each: $\int (f + g) \le \int f + \int g$. Signed bounded cases split into parts, all finite on finite ground. *Dividend banked: every use in Theorems 4.19 and 4.20 cites this problem.*

**II.3 (solution in full).** *Monotonicity of the step sandwiches.* $P_{n+1}$ refines $P_n$: each $P_{n+1}$-slice sits inside a $P_n$-slice, so slice-infima rise ($\varphi_{n+1} \ge \varphi_n$) and slice-suprema fall, pointwise off the (countable, null) set of all partition points — where values may be redefined freely under the a.e. dialect (Proposition 4.16). *Limits.* Monotone bounded sequences converge pointwise (Volume One, MCT for sequences); $\varphi, \psi$ measurable by Theorem 4.6. *The pinch.* $\int(\psi - \varphi) \le \int (\psi_n - \varphi_n) = U - L \to 0$ uses monotonicity of the integral on the nonnegative differences (Proposition 4.13(i)) and bounded additivity (II.2) to split $\int \psi_n - \int \varphi_n$; I.6 then forces $\psi = \varphi$ a.e.; amnesty passes measurability to $f$; and $\int f = \int \varphi = \lim L(f, P_n) = R$, the middle step because $\varphi_n \le \varphi \le \psi_n$ pinches $\int \varphi$ between $L(f, P_n)$ and $U(f, P_n)$.

#### 5.2 The Climbing License

> **Theorem 5.1 (Monotone convergence — Levi, 1906).** Let $f_n : E \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable with $f_n \le f_{n+1}$ pointwise and $f_n \to f$ pointwise. Then $f$ is measurable and
>
> $$\int_E f_n \, dm \ \uparrow\ \int_E f \, dm .$$
>
> (A.e. monotonicity and convergence suffice: patch the null set, Proposition 4.16.)

*Proof.* $f$ is measurable as a pointwise limit (Theorem 4.6). *Free half:* $f_n \le f$ gives $\int f_n \le \int f$ (manners); the integrals climb (monotonicity again), so $L = \lim_n \int f_n$ exists in $[0, \infty]$ with $L \le \int f$.

*Substance.* Fix a simple $\varphi$ with $0 \le \varphi \le f$ and a discount $c \in (0, 1)$; write $\varphi = \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i \mathbf{1}_{A_i}$. The sufficiency sets

$$E_n \ =\ \{ x \in E : f_n(x) \ge c\,\varphi(x) \}$$

are citizens ($f_n - c\varphi$ measurable), swell with $n$ (the climb), and exhaust $E$: where $\varphi(x) = 0$ membership is immediate; where $\varphi(x) > 0$, $c \varphi(x) < \varphi(x) \le f(x)$, so some $f_n(x)$ has cleared $c \varphi(x)$. Then

$$\int f_n \ \ge\ \int_{E_n} f_n \ \ge\ c \int_{E_n} \varphi \ =\ c \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i \, m(A_i \cap E_n) \ \xrightarrow[n \to \infty]{}\ c \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i \, m(A_i) \ =\ c \int \varphi,$$

the arrow by the crankshaft (continuity along swelling chains, Proposition 1.3(i)) applied to each of the finitely many storeys $A_i \cap E_n \uparrow A_i$. Hence $L \ge c \int \varphi$ for every $c < 1$: $L \ge \int \varphi$ (let the discount expire); and taking the supremum over under-staircases, $L \ge \int f$ by ring sixteen's definition. With the free half, $L = \int f$. ∎

> **Remark 5.2 (The sign clause; the improper absorption).** Signed climbing fails: $f_n = -\tfrac1x \mathbf{1}_{(0, 1/n)}$-style descending starts have $\int f_n = -\infty$ throughout while the limit vanishes; a finite first floor restores the mirror (Problem I.8, the descending tower). *Absorption:* for measurable $f \ge 0$ on $(0, 1]$ with improper Riemann integral finite, the truncations $f \mathbf{1}_{[1/n, 1]}$ climb to $f$; each truncated integral is Riemann's (Chapter 4's absorption on the frame); MCT passes the limit — e.g. $\int_{(0,1]} x^{-1/2} \, dm = \lim_n (2 - 2/\sqrt{n}) = 2$. Chapter 4's boundary post, absolutely convergent half: retired.

> **Corollary 5.3 (Additivity — debt fourteen discharged).** For measurable $f, g \ge 0$: $\int (f + g) = \int f + \int g$; hence for integrable $f, g$ and scalars, the integral is linear.

*Proof.* Staircases $\varphi_n \uparrow f$, $\psi_n \uparrow g$ (Theorem 4.9); $\varphi_n + \psi_n \uparrow f + g$; simple additivity (Proposition 4.8) and Theorem 5.1 on all three sequences pass the identity through the limit. The signed case splits into parts, every term finite by integrability. *The one-week credit (Remark 4.15) is retired on schedule.* ∎

> **Corollary 5.4 (Nonnegative series swap freely).** For measurable $f_k \ge 0$: $\displaystyle \int \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} f_k \, dm = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \int f_k \, dm$ (both sides possibly $\infty$, together).

*Proof.* Partial sums climb; Corollary 5.3 prices each; Theorem 5.1 passes the limit. ∎

#### 5.3 The One-Way Valve

> **Theorem 5.5 (Fatou, 1906).** For measurable $f_n \ge 0$:
>
> $$\int \liminf_n f_n \, dm \ \le\ \liminf_n \int f_n \, dm .$$

*Proof.* $g_n = \inf_{k \ge n} f_k$ is measurable (Theorem 4.6), climbs, and $g_n \uparrow \liminf f_n$ by definition. From $g_n \le f_n$: $\int g_n \le \int f_n$, so $\lim \int g_n \le \liminf \int f_n$ (the left limit exists: MCT's free half). MCT prices the left limit as $\int \liminf f_n$. ∎

> **Remark 5.6 (Cautions).** Strictness: the spike ($\liminf = 0$; integrals $= 1$). No unsigned valve: the negative spike $-n \mathbf{1}_{(0, 1/n)}$ has $\int \liminf = 0 > -1 = \liminf \int$ read against the claimed direction — the sign gasket is structural. No limsup mirror without a lid: the bump has $\int \limsup = 0 < 1 = \limsup \int$; with an integrable lid $g$, the reverse valve holds ($\limsup \int f_n \le \int \limsup f_n$, by Theorem 5.5 on $g - f_n$ — Problem II.3's ambit).

#### 5.4 The Crown Jewel

> **Proposition 5.7 (No lids over the escapes).** Any measurable $g$ dominating all bumps has $g \ge \mathbf{1}_{[0, \infty)}$ a.e.-eventually in the obvious sense and $\int g = \infty$; dominating all spikes forces $g(x) \ge \sup_n n \mathbf{1}_{(0,1/n)}(x)$, which exceeds $\tfrac{1}{2x}$ near nought; dominating all spreads forces $g \ge \tfrac1n$ on $[0, n]$ for all $n$, whence $\int g \ge \sum_n \tfrac1n \cdot 1$-flavoured lower bounds diverge (the desk's one-line versions: Problem I.4). No integrable lid exists in any of the three galleries.

*Proof.* Problem I.4, with the harmonic comparison for the spread and the $1/(2x)$ comparison for the spike (between $1/(k+1)$ and $1/k$ the sup of spikes is at least $k \ge 1/(2x)$). ∎

> **Theorem 5.8 (Dominated convergence — Lebesgue).** Let $f_n$ be measurable, $f_n \to f$ a.e., and $\lvert f_n \rvert \le g$ a.e. for every $n$, with $g$ integrable. Then $f$ is integrable and $\int f_n \, dm \to \int f \, dm$.

*Proof.* Patch the null exceptions (the amnesty); assume the hypotheses everywhere. $\lvert f \rvert \le g$ in the limit: $f$ integrable with room ($\int \lvert f \rvert \le \int g < \infty$). The sequences $g + f_n \ge 0$ and $g - f_n \ge 0$ are lawful valve inputs. Fatou on the first:

$$\int g + \int f \ =\ \int (g + f) \ \le\ \liminf \int (g + f_n) \ =\ \int g + \liminf \int f_n ,$$

additivity (Corollary 5.3) expanding both ends; *cancel $\int g$ — finite, the lid's integrability spent, first time*: $\int f \le \liminf \int f_n$. Fatou on the second, the same bookkeeping (*the second expenditure*): $\int g - \int f \le \int g - \limsup \int f_n$, i.e. $\limsup \int f_n \le \int f$. The pinch closes: $\lim \int f_n = \int f$. ∎

> **Corollary 5.9 (The mean-convergence rider).** Under Theorem 5.8's hypotheses, $\int \lvert f_n - f \rvert \, dm \to 0$.

*Proof.* $\lvert f_n - f \rvert \to 0$ a.e., dominated by $2g$; Theorem 5.8 applied to the discrepancies. ∎

> **Corollary 5.10 (Bounded convergence — probability's workhorse).** On $E$ with $m(E) < \infty$: if $f_n \to f$ a.e. and $\lvert f_n \rvert \le M$ (one constant, all $n$), then $\int f_n \to \int f$.

*Proof.* $g = M \mathbf{1}_E$ is integrable on finite ground; the jewel applies. ∎

> **Remark 5.11 (Season One's finale theorem, retired with honours).** Volume One, Chapter 8's interchange theorem (uniform convergence on $[a,b]$ licenses the swap) is now two lines: uniform convergence eventually pins $\lvert f_n \rvert \le \lvert f \rvert + 1 \le M+1$ — $f$ bounded as a uniform limit of bounded functions — a constant lid on finite ground; Corollary 5.10. The spread (Remark 5.12) marks where the retirement's finite-ground clause was always working.

> **Remark 5.12 (The spread).** $\tfrac1n \mathbf{1}_{[0,n]} \rightrightarrows 0$ uniformly, yet $\int = 1 \not\to 0$: on infinite ground, uniformity neither implies domination nor substitutes for it (the failing line of the old proof: the tube's cross-section times the ground's width, $\tfrac1n \cdot n$, refuses to vanish). Problem II.5 dissects.

#### 5.5 What the Lid Buys

> **Theorem 5.13 (Continuity in a parameter).** Let $f(x, t)$ be measurable in $x$ for each $t$ in an interval, continuous in $t$ for a.e. $x$, and dominated: $\lvert f(x, t) \rvert \le g(x)$, $g$ integrable, for all $t$. Then $F(t) = \int f(x, t) \, dm(x)$ is continuous.

*Proof.* Sequential continuity suffices (Volume One): $t_k \to t$ gives $f(x, t_k) \to f(x, t)$ a.e., dominated by $g$; Theorem 5.8. ∎

> **Theorem 5.14 (Differentiation under the integral sign).** Let $f(x, t)$ be integrable in $x$ for each $t$ in an open interval, differentiable in $t$ for a.e. $x$, with the derivative dominated: $\lvert \partial_t f(x, t) \rvert \le g(x)$, $g$ integrable, for all $t$ in the interval. Then $F(t) = \int f(x, t)\, dm(x)$ is differentiable, and
>
> $$F'(t) \ =\ \int \partial_t f(x, t) \, dm(x).$$

*Proof.* Fix $t$; take any $h_k \to 0$. The quotients $q_k(x) = \bigl( f(x, t + h_k) - f(x, t) \bigr) / h_k$ converge a.e. to $\partial_t f(x, t)$; *the mean-value bridge*: for each $x$ and $k$, Volume One's mean value theorem plants a witness $s$ between $t$ and $t + h_k$ with $q_k(x) = \partial_t f(x, s)$, so $\lvert q_k(x) \rvert \le g(x)$ — the derivative's lid covers every quotient. Theorem 5.8 passes the limit through the integral; linearity identifies the quotient of $F$ with $\int q_k$. Every sequence $h_k$ agreeing, $F'(t)$ exists and equals the display. ∎

> **Remark 5.15 (The parade, tabulated).**
> | **Specimen** | **Violated clause** | **Failure** |
> | --- | --- | --- |
> | bump | MCT's climb; DCT's lid | $\int \to 1 \ne 0$ |
> | [2pt] spike | the lid ($\ge 1/2x$) | $\int = 1$, limit $0$; Fatou strict |
> | [2pt] spread | the lid (harmonic); uniformity no substitute | $\int = 1 \ne 0$ despite $\rightrightarrows$ |
> | [2pt] negative spike | Fatou's sign | valve leaks backward |
> | [2pt] descending tower | finite first floor | signed climb, $\int \equiv -\infty$ |
>
> Each hypothesis of each license, violated exactly once; no theorem wounded.

> **Remark 5.16 (Debt five: the account, closed).** Opened S1E4 (the rearrangement); instalment one S1E7 (limits past limits, uniformly); instalment two S1E8 (limit past integral, uniformly, stinginess codicil filed); closed tonight: climbing, nonnegative, or dominated mass swaps freely on any measurable ground. The codicil is discharged with prejudice — Remark 5.11 prices the old license as a pocket corollary. *Converted into standing law.*

#### 5.8 Solutions

**Tier I (terse).** **I.1**–**I.8** As drilled; I.8's mirror: if $f_n \downarrow f \ge 0$ pointwise with $\int f_1 < \infty$, then $\int f_n \downarrow \int f$ (apply Theorem 5.8 with lid $f_1$, or the crankshaft on complements).

**II.1 (solution in full).** As Theorem 5.1's substance, expanded: fix $\varphi, c$; the sets $E_n$ swell and exhaust (two cases displayed); for each storey, $m(A_i \cap E_n) \uparrow m(A_i)$ is Proposition 1.3(i) applied to the swelling chain $A_i \cap E_n$ (citizens, intersections); summing finitely many storeys preserves the limit (Volume One's algebra of limits); whence $L \ge c \int \varphi$; the map $c \mapsto c \int \varphi$ is continuous on $(0,1)$ with supremum $\int \varphi$ (or: given $\varepsilon$, pick $c > 1 - \varepsilon / (1 + \int \varphi)$ when $\int \varphi < \infty$, and any $c$ with $c \int \varphi > M$ arbitrary when $\int \varphi = \infty$); the under-staircase supremum closes onto ring sixteen's definition.

**II.2 (solution in full).** As Theorem 5.8, with the ledger: integrability of $f$ from the limit lid; nonnegativity of $g \pm f_n$ from the domination; additivity's two expansions (Corollary 5.3, tonight's discharge — the proof is not circular: the corollary rests on MCT alone); the two cancellations, each a subtraction of the *finite* $\int g$ (the season's one prohibition respected — this is where integrability of the lid is spent, and the proof collapses without it: take $g = \infty$-flavoured lids and the inequalities read $\infty \le \infty$, empty); the final pinch $\limsup \le \int f \le \liminf$.

### Chapter 6. The Zoo of Convergence, or Littlewood's Three Principles

*Companion to Episode Six. The episode read Littlewood's three principles as field guide, paraded the five modes with their working currencies, walked the implication map compass in hand, staged the typewriter (wonder beat: "you can hear the carriage return"), extracted the subsequence consolation with its Borel–Cantelli skeleton flagged for the finale, proved Egorov aloud in strategy (shrinking crankshaft + the gambit), assembled Lusin from three nearlies, built the mean distance (amnesty as geometry), rang **ring seventeen** at Riesz–Fischer on ring twelve's precedent, and exiled Hölder and Minkowski by name — "the honest division of labour is not a compromise; it is the design." This chapter is the paperwork; its core is the diagram with a proof or a counterexample on every arrow, per the plan's mandate. Register notes: the bell rings once — $(\circledast)$ at Theorem 6.10, flagged for veto, precedent Volume One's ring twelve.*

#### Episode Digest

**The argument of the hour.** Five modes, one map, three principles. Uniform, pointwise, almost-everywhere, in-the-mean, in-measure — each the currency of a working question (guarantees, trajectories, expected loss, consistency). The map: uniform at the headwaters; mean $\to$ measure by Chebyshev's embryo (mass bounds acreage); a.e. $\to$ measure on finite ground (the bump patrols the frontier); mean and a.e. incomparable (the spike one way, the typewriter the other). The typewriter — blocks sweeping the interval in halving generations — converges in measure and mean, pointwise nowhere: smallness of offence and persistence of offence are different failures. In-measure extracts a.e. along a fast subsequence (the gambit + tail-trap; Borel–Cantelli in embryo). Egorov: on finite ground, a.e. convergence is uniform off epsilon acreage (shrinking crankshaft, finite floor cited; the bump witnesses the clause). Lusin: measurable functions are continuous off epsilon acreage (restriction, not pointwise — the static on the irrationals pins the distinction; the property characterizes measurability); assembled from staircases + the first principle + Egorov + the three-legged stool. The mean distance makes the integrable functions a space (points = a.e.-classes); Riesz–Fischer: it is complete — fast subsequence, stacked series, climbing license, dominated closure — ring seventeen on ring twelve's precedent. Hölder and Minkowski: named, motivated, exiled; proved at the desk via Young.

**The episode, beat by beat.**

**The Field Guide / The Modes in the Wild.** The three principles; "nearly" as exact currency; the five modes' working questions.

**The Five Modes / The Geography.** Definitions (Definition 6.1); the walked map; Chebyshev's embryo (Lemma 6.2); the full diagram (Theorem 6.3).

**The Typewriter.** Construction and both verdicts (Proposition 6.4); the wonder beat.

**Egorov's Theorem.** Theorem 6.7; the finite floor at its line; the bump as witness.

**Lusin's Theorem.** Statement and footnotes (Theorem 6.8, sketch with references per plan); the characterization remark.

**The Mean as a Distance / Riesz–Fischer.** The space $L^1$ (Definition 6.9); $(\circledast)$ Theorem 6.10, the guided centrepiece solved in full.

**The Exiles.** Young, Hölder, Minkowski (Theorems 6.11–6.13); the $L^p$ glimpse and nesting.

**The toolkit acquired.** The exchange-rate map; the fast-subsequence harvest; the shrinking-tails manoeuvre; amnesty-as-geometry; the exile discipline.

**Dates worth keeping.** Riesz and Fischer, independently, 1907, both via Fourier series; Egorov, 1911; Lusin, 1912; Littlewood's principles as printed maxims, 1944 (*Lectures on the Theory of Functions*).

#### 6.2 The Map

> **Definition 6.1 (The two integral modes).** On measurable ground $E$: $f_n \to f$ *in the mean* when $\int_E \lvert f_n - f \rvert \, dm \to 0$; *in measure* when for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $m\{ x \in E : \lvert f_n(x) - f(x) \rvert \ge \varepsilon \} \to 0$. (Uniform, pointwise, and a.e. are of long standing.)

> **Lemma 6.2 (Chebyshev's embryo: mass bounds acreage).** For measurable $g \ge 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$: $m\{ g \ge \varepsilon \} \le \tfrac{1}{\varepsilon} \int g \, dm$.

*Proof.* $\varepsilon \, \mathbf{1}_{\{g \ge \varepsilon\}} \le g$ pointwise; integrate (manners, Chapter 4). The finale christens the general form. ∎

> **Theorem 6.3 (The diagram, every arrow warranted).** On ground $E$:
>
> 1. **(i)** uniform $\Rightarrow$ pointwise $\Rightarrow$ a.e.; uniform $\Rightarrow$ mean when $m(E) < \infty$ ($\lVert f_n - f \rVert_1 \le d(f_n, f) \, m(E)$); the spread kills the finiteness clause.
> 1. **(ii)** mean $\Rightarrow$ measure, always (Lemma 6.2 on $\lvert f_n - f \rvert$).
> 1. **(iii)** a.e. $\Rightarrow$ measure when $m(E) < \infty$ (via Theorem 6.7: off acreage $\varepsilon$ the discrepancy is eventually uniform, hence eventually below $\varepsilon$ everywhere there; the offending ground is eventually inside the sacrificed acreage). The bump kills the clause on infinite ground.
> 1. **(iv)** mean $\not\Rightarrow$ a.e. (the typewriter, Proposition 6.4); a.e. $\not\Rightarrow$ mean (the spike); measure $\not\Rightarrow$ a.e. (typewriter); measure $\not\Rightarrow$ mean (spike, which converges in measure); pointwise $\not\Rightarrow$ uniform (Volume One's ramps); a.e. $\not\Rightarrow$ pointwise (redefine on $\Q$).
>
> The five-by-five table with one-line warrants is Problem I.1's completed grid.

*Proof.* All displayed; (iii)'s derivation from Egorov is Problem II.1, solved in full, with the bump's frontier patrol. ∎

> **Proposition 6.4 (The typewriter).** For $n = 2^k + j$, $0 \le j < 2^k$, let $T_n = \mathbf{1}_{[j 2^{-k}, (j+1) 2^{-k}]}$ on $[0, 1]$. Then $T_n \to 0$ in measure and in the mean ($m(\mathrm{supp}\, T_n) = \int T_n = 2^{-k} \to 0$), and $(T_n(x))$ converges for *no* $x \in [0,1]$: each generation's carriage passes every point once, so $T_n(x) = 1$ infinitely often and $T_n(x) = 0$ infinitely often.

*Proof.* The two computations are displayed; the pointwise verdict is Problem II.2, solved in full (for each $k$ there is exactly one $j$ with $x \in [j 2^{-k}, (j+1) 2^{-k}]$ — two at a dyadic seam, which only helps — so ones recur eternally; zeros recur since $2^k > 1$ blocks per generation miss $x$). ∎

> **Theorem 6.5 (The consolation: a.e. along a subsequence).** If $f_n \to f$ in measure on $E$, there are indices $n_1 < n_2 < \cdots$ with $f_{n_k} \to f$ almost everywhere.

*Proof.* Harvest: choose $n_k$ with $m(A_k) \le 2^{-k}$ for $A_k = \{ \lvert f_{n_k} - f \rvert \ge 2^{-k} \}$ (in-measure convergence supplies each). Tail-trap: let $B_K = \bigcup_{k \ge K} A_k$, so $m(B_K) \le 2^{1-K}$ (the gambit's series), and $N = \bigcap_K B_K$ is null. Off $N$: $x$ eventually avoids every $A_k$ beyond some $K$, so $\lvert f_{n_k}(x) - f(x) \rvert < 2^{-k}$ for all $k \ge K$: convergence. ∎

> **Remark 6.6 (The skeleton, flagged).** The step "summable acreages $\Rightarrow$ the visited-infinitely-often set is null" is the first Borel–Cantelli lemma, proved here in embryo; the finale states it under its name and spends it on almost-sure convergence. A converse service: if every subsequence of $(f_n)$ has a further subsequence converging a.e. to $f$, then $f_n \to f$ in measure (Problem II.4 — the trade's standard trick for upgrading subsequential verdicts).

> **Theorem 6.7 (Egorov, 1911).** Let $m(E) < \infty$ and $f_n \to f$ a.e. on $E$, all measurable and finite a.e. For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a citizen $A \subseteq E$ with $m(E \setminus A) < \varepsilon$ and $f_n \rightrightarrows f$ on $A$.

*Proof.* For $k, n \in \N$ let $E_{n,k} = \bigcup_{m \ge n} \{ \lvert f_m - f \rvert > \tfrac1k \}$: citizens, shrinking in $n$. Their intersection over $n$ is contained in the null non-convergence set (a point in every $E_{n,k}$ suffers $\tfrac1k$-discrepancies beyond every stage), so, *the finite floor being available* ($m(E) < \infty$ — the crankshaft's shrinking clause, Proposition 1.3(ii), spent here and nowhere else), $m(E_{n,k}) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. Choose $n_k$ with $m(E_{n_k, k}) < \varepsilon 2^{-k}$ (the gambit); set $A = E \setminus \bigcup_k E_{n_k, k}$, so $m(E \setminus A) < \varepsilon$. On $A$: for every $k$ and every $m \ge n_k$, $\lvert f_m - f \rvert \le \tfrac1k$ — one threshold per tolerance, valid across all of $A$: uniform convergence. The bump on $[0, \infty)$ converges everywhere yet is uniform on no co-finite-acreage set (its unit block always escapes any fixed bounded remainder): the finiteness clause is real. ∎

> **Theorem 6.8 (Lusin, 1912 — sketched, with references).** Let $f$ be measurable and finite a.e. on $[a,b]$. For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a closed $F \subseteq [a,b]$ with $m([a,b] \setminus F) < \varepsilon$ such that the restriction $f\restriction_F$ is continuous. Moreover the property characterizes measurability.

*Assembly (the three nearlies, epsilons split by the gambit).* Staircases $\varphi_j \to f$ a.e. (Theorem 4.9); each $\varphi_j$ is continuous off open acreage $\varepsilon 2^{-j-1}$ — its finitely many storeys are nearly finite unions of intervals (Littlewood's first principle, Chapter 2's manners, Problem II.4 there), and off the boundary slivers the storey structure is locally constant; Egorov (Theorem 6.7) makes $\varphi_j \to f$ uniform off acreage $\varepsilon / 4$; a uniform limit of continuous restrictions is continuous (Volume One's three-legged stool, on the restricted set); the closed certificate comes from inner regularity (Chapter 2). Full details: Axler 2D, Royden ch. 3, Stein–Shakarchi ch. 1; the characterization converse: Problem III.1's references. *Footnote pinned in the episode: continuity of the restriction, not continuity at points — the static restricted to the irrationals is identically $0$.*

#### 6.3 The Mean Distance and Riesz–Fischer

> **Definition 6.9 ($L^1$; the mean distance).** $L^1(E)$: the integrable functions on $E$, identified when equal a.e. (the amnesty as geometry: distance-zero pairs are one point); $d_1(f, g) = \int_E \lvert f - g \rvert \, dm$. Metric axioms: symmetry and nonnegativity are manifest; $d_1(f,g) = 0$ iff $f = g$ a.e. (Chapter 4's little lemma, I.6); the triangle inequality is additivity on the pointwise triangle $\lvert f - h \rvert \le \lvert f - g \rvert + \lvert g - h \rvert$.

> **Theorem 6.10 ($(\circledast)$ Riesz–Fischer, 1907 — ring seventeen).** $L^1(E)$ is complete: every Cauchy sequence in the mean distance converges in the mean to a member of $L^1(E)$.

*Proof.* (The guided centrepiece, solved in full; each jewel cited at its expenditure.) Let $(f_n)$ be $d_1$-Cauchy. *Harvest* $n_k$ with $d_1(f_{n_{k+1}}, f_{n_k}) \le 2^{-k}$ (Cauchy supplies; the gambit's rates). *Stack*: let $g = \lvert f_{n_1} \rvert + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \lvert f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k} \rvert$, a nonnegative measurable function; the climbing license through the series corollary (Corollary 5.4) prices $\int g \le \int \lvert f_{n_1} \rvert + \sum_k 2^{-k} < \infty$: $g$ is integrable, hence finite a.e. *Limit*: where $g$ is finite, the telescoping series $f_{n_1} + \sum_k (f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k})$ converges absolutely (Volume One's comparison against the stack); call the a.e. limit $f$ — measurable (Theorem 4.6), and $\lvert f \rvert \le g$: integrable. *Closure*: $\lvert f - f_{n_k} \rvert \le \sum_{j \ge k} \lvert f_{n_{j+1}} - f_{n_j} \rvert \le g$ with a.e. convergence to $0$; the dominated jewel's rider (Corollary 5.9, via Theorem 5.8 with lid $g$) gives $d_1(f, f_{n_k}) \to 0$; and a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges (Volume One's huddle lemma, verbatim in any metric): $d_1(f, f_n) \to 0$. *The bell rings — the seventeenth*: the completeness of the space in which twentieth-century analysis lives, on the precedent of ring twelve (Volume One's $C$ under the uniform distance); flagged for veto, per standing practice. ∎

#### 6.4 The Exiles

> **Theorem 6.11 (Young's inequality).** Let $p, q \in (1, \infty)$ with $\tfrac1p + \tfrac1q = 1$. For $a, b \ge 0$: $ab \le \tfrac{a^p}{p} + \tfrac{b^q}{q}$, with equality iff $a^p = b^q$.

*Proof.* Fix $b \ge 0$ and maximize $h(a) = ab - a^p / p$ over $a \ge 0$: $h'(a) = b - a^{p-1}$ vanishes at $a_* = b^{1/(p-1)} = b^{q-1}$ — a maximum, $h''< 0$ (Volume One's harvest). Then $h(a_*) = b^{q-1} b - b^{(q-1)p}/p = b^q (1 - \tfrac1p) = b^q / q$, using $(q-1)p = q$. So $ab - a^p/p \le b^q / q$ for all $a$, which is the claim; equality exactly at $a = a_*$, i.e. $a^p = b^q$. (No logarithms; the credit stands unspent.) ∎

> **Theorem 6.12 (Hölder's inequality).** With $p, q$ conjugate and $f, g$ measurable:
>
> $$\int \lvert f g \rvert \, dm \ \le\ \Bigl( \int \lvert f \rvert^p \Bigr)^{1/p} \Bigl( \int \lvert g \rvert^q \Bigr)^{1/q} \ =\ \lVert f \rVert_p \, \lVert g \rVert_q .$$

*Proof.* If either norm is $0$ or $\infty$, the desk's two-line cases settle it (a null factor annihilates; an infinite bound is vacuous). Otherwise normalize: $u = \lvert f \rvert / \lVert f \rVert_p$, $v = \lvert g \rvert / \lVert g \rVert_q$; Young pointwise: $uv \le u^p / p + v^q / q$; integrate (additivity): $\int uv \le \tfrac1p + \tfrac1q = 1$; unnormalize. ∎

> **Theorem 6.13 (Minkowski's inequality).** $\lVert f + g \rVert_p \le \lVert f \rVert_p + \lVert g \rVert_p$ for $1 \le p < \infty$.

*Proof.* $p = 1$ is additivity on the pointwise triangle. For $p > 1$:

$$\int \lvert f + g \rvert^p \le \int \lvert f \rvert \, \lvert f + g \rvert^{p-1} + \int \lvert g \rvert \, \lvert f + g \rvert^{p-1} \le \bigl( \lVert f \rVert_p + \lVert g \rVert_p \bigr) \, \bigl\lVert \, \lvert f+g \rvert^{p-1} \bigr\rVert_q$$

by the pointwise triangle then Hölder twice; and $\lVert \lvert f+g \rvert^{p-1} \rVert_q = ( \int \lvert f+g \rvert^p )^{1/q}$ since $(p-1)q = p$. Divide (finiteness first: $\lvert f + g \rvert^p \le 2^p (\lvert f \rvert^p + \lvert g \rvert^p)$ keeps the divisor finite; zero divisor: nothing to prove). ∎

> **Remark 6.14 (The $L^p$ glimpse).** On finite ground, $L^p \subseteq L^r$ for $p > r$ (Hölder with exponent $p/r$ against the constant one: Problem I.8); the family's completeness generalizes Theorem 6.10 (Problem III.1). The course's boundary: duality, Hilbert space, and Fourier's settlement belong to a further season; the Notes point onward.

#### 6.6 Hints

**II.4.** If $f_n \not\to f$ in measure: some $\varepsilon_0, \delta_0$ and indices $n_j$ with $m\{\lvert f_{n_j} - f \rvert \ge \varepsilon_0\} \ge \delta_0$; no further subsequence can converge a.e. (it would converge in measure on the finite frame trapping $\delta_0$ of the acreage — II.1).

**III.2.** In a metric space, $x_n \to x$ iff every subsequence has a sub-subsequence $\to x$; the typewriter violates the conclusion while satisfying the premise for a.e.-mode.

#### 6.7 Solutions

**Tier I (terse).** **I.1** Grid as in Theorem 6.3; the spread's line: uniform yes, pointwise yes, a.e. yes, mean no, measure yes (acreage $\{ \tfrac1n \ge \varepsilon \}$ is empty for large $n$ — note it converges in measure though not in mean). **I.5** $A = [\tfrac1{10}, 1]$: beyond $n = 10$ the spike's support misses $A$; threshold $N = 10$ for every tolerance. **I.7** $d_1(D, 0) = 0$ — the static IS the zero of $L^1$: one point of the space, the amnesty as geometry made vivid; $d_1(t, 0) = 0$ likewise; two generation-$k$ blocks: $2 \cdot 2^{-k}$ when disjoint. **I.8** $\lVert f \rVert_1 = \int \lvert f \rvert \cdot 1 \le \lVert f \rVert_2 \lVert 1 \rVert_2 = \lVert f \rVert_2$; on $[0,\infty)$: $f = \tfrac1x \mathbf{1}_{[1,\infty)}$ has $\lVert f \rVert_2 < \infty = \lVert f \rVert_1$.

**II.1 (solution in full).** Let $m(E) < \infty$, $f_n \to f$ a.e., $\varepsilon > 0$, $\delta > 0$. Egorov supplies $A$ with $m(E \setminus A) < \delta$ and uniform convergence on $A$: beyond some $N$, $\lvert f_n - f \rvert < \varepsilon$ on all of $A$, so $\{ \lvert f_n - f \rvert \ge \varepsilon \} \subseteq E \setminus A$ for $n \ge N$: acreage below $\delta$. As $\delta$ was arbitrary, the acreage tends to $0$: in-measure convergence. The bump: $\{ \lvert \mathbf{1}_{[n, n+1]} \rvert \ge \tfrac12 \}$ has measure $1$ for every $n$ — the arrow dies without the finite floor, and Egorov's own hypothesis was the casualty (Problem II.3).

**II.2 (solution in full).** Fix $x \in [0,1]$ and a generation $k$. The blocks $[j 2^{-k}, (j+1) 2^{-k}]$, $j = 0, \dots, 2^k - 1$, cover $[0,1]$, so some $j$ has $x$ in its block: $T_{2^k + j}(x) = 1$. Ones occur in every generation: infinitely often. For zeros: $2^k \ge 2$ blocks exist from generation one onward and at most two contain $x$ (a seam), so some block misses $x$: $T_n(x) = 0$ infinitely often. A sequence with both values infinitely often has no limit; no $x$ is spared, seams included. (The subsequence of first blocks $T_{2^k}$ converges to $0$ at every $x > 0$: the consolation prize's illustration.)

### Chapter 7. Fubini, or the Crime of Swapping Integrals

*Companion to Episode Seven. The episode built the plane from two lines (rectangles, the product tribe, Carathéodory rerun; the two routes agreeing), sharpened both knives (sections, with the monotone-class beam flagged honestly as the season's one labelled borrowing), proved Tonelli by the four-stage reel (rectangles, tribe, staircases, climb), derived Fubini by gains and losses, canonized the standard operating procedure (check with Tonelli, spend with Fubini), convicted the staircase-and-shadows function at the crime scene (both itineraries computed; diagnosis: Season One's rearrangement crime in planar dress), witnessed the sigma-finite fine print at the counting-measure diagonal, and banked the layer cake (wonder beat: the two seasons' pictures of an integral meeting in the subgraph). This chapter is the paperwork. Register notes: **the bell is silent** — count holds at seventeen; the product construction reruns architecture already rung. The SOP promise of Chapter 5 is discharged at Remark 7.9.*

#### Episode Digest

**The argument of the hour.** When may a double integral be computed in either order? Build the plane honestly: rectangle atoms priced by the area rule; the product tribe generated from above; the product measure by Carathéodory on rectangle covers, unique by the frame squeeze, agreeing with the direct planar construction. Sections are measurable (the monotone-class beam, labelled). Tonelli: nonnegative functions swap freely, always — rectangles agree by inspection, the beam carries agreement to the tribe, staircases and the climbing license carry it to everything. Fubini: integrable functions swap after the absolute check, bad slices null and amnestied. The SOP canonized. The crime scene: the diagonal staircase with rightward shadows — columns total one then nought (the ground floor casts no shadow into itself), rows total nought without exception; iterated integrals one and nought, both finite, both correct; absolute mass infinite; the rearrangement theorem in planar dress. Fine print: sigma-finiteness (the counting-measure diagonal: nonnegative, measurable, itineraries nought and one). The layer cake: integrate the subgraph's indicator both ways — vertical slices give the integral, horizontal slices give the acreage-above-height — Tonelli's somersault; the bridge to tail probabilities pre-signed for the finale.

| [2pt] "the subgraph" | $S_f = \{ (x, t) : 0 \le t < f(x) \}$ | Thm. 7.12 |

#### 7.2 The Product Construction

> **Definition 7.1 (Rectangles).** A *measurable rectangle* is $A \times B$ with $A, B \in \mathcal{M}$ (on the two factor lines), priced $\rho(A \times B) = m(A) \, m(B)$ (extended arithmetic; $0 \cdot \infty = 0$).

> **Theorem 7.2 (The product measure).** On $\mathcal{M} \otimes \mathcal{M} = \sigma(\{\text{rectangles}\})$ there is a measure $m \times m$ agreeing with $\rho$ on rectangles; on sigma-finite factors (our case) it is the unique such.

*Proof.* Existence: run Carathéodory on countable rectangle covers — define the planar outer measure as the infimum of $\sum_k \rho(R_k)$ over rectangle covers; the 1914 staircase (Chapter 2, quoted, not re-proved: symmetry, composition, proportion, limit) yields a sigma-algebra of splitters carrying a countably additive restriction; rectangles split cleanly (the half-plane turnstiles $A \times \R$ and $\R \times B$ mirror Chapter 2's half-lines — Problem II.1 performs the audit), so the splitters include the rectangles, hence the generated tribe. That $\rho$ is itself countably additive on rectangles — the covering bound needs it — is Problem II.1's second half, a Tonelli-in- miniature for indicator slices (or: the desk's direct route via the line's MCT on sections of a disjoint rectangle union). Uniqueness: two agreeing measures on rectangles agree on finite frames $[-N,N]^2$ by the frame squeeze of Chapter 2's uniqueness theorem transplanted verbatim (rectangles play intervals; the estate's robustness plays itself), and sigma-finiteness patches the frames by the crankshaft. ∎

> **Corollary 7.3 (The two routes agree).** The direct planar Lebesgue measure (Chapter 2's dimension license) and $m \times m$ coincide on the product tribe.

*Proof.* Both keep the rectangle clause (boxes are rectangles; the direct construction prices boxes by area — its own interval theorem run twice); uniqueness closes. (The product tribe sits inside the direct construction's full commonwealth; on the common jurisdiction they agree, and the completion remark of the Notes handles the veil.) ∎

> **Definition 7.4 (Sections).** For $E$ in the plane and $y$ fixed: $E^{y} = \{ x : (x,y) \in E \}$; dually $E_{x}$. For functions: $f^{y}(x) = f(x, y)$, $f_{x}(y) = f(x, y)$.

> **Lemma 7.5 (Sections are measurable).** If $E \in \mathcal{M} \otimes \mathcal{M}$, every section $E^{y}, E_{x}$ is a citizen of its line; if $f$ is product-measurable, every section function is measurable.

> **Remark 7.6 (The monotone-class beam — the labelled borrowing).** The collection of sets with all sections measurable contains the rectangles ($ (A \times B)^{y}$ is $A$ or $\emptyset$) and is a sigma-algebra (sections commute with complements and countable unions — the accessible half, proved here in four lines: $(\bigcup_k E_k)^{y} = \bigcup_k E_k^{y}$ and $(E^{c})^{y} = (E^{y})^{c}$); hence it contains the generated tribe, and Lemma 7.5 follows — *for sets*. For the *measure-theoretic* upgrades Tonelli's stage two needs — that $y \mapsto m(E^{y})$ is measurable with $\int m(E^{y}) \, dm(y) = (m \times m)(E)$ — the standard induction over the tribe wants the *monotone class theorem*: stated here (a monotone class containing an algebra contains its generated sigma-algebra), its proof cited to the shelves (Folland §2.1; Axler 5A; Royden ch. 20) per the plan's instruction to flag the machinery honestly. The sigma-finite bookkeeping of the induction is Problem III.1's guided skeleton. *One beam, borrowed, labelled; everything else in the chapter is house timber.*

#### 7.3 The Matched Pair

> **Theorem 7.7 (Tonelli, 1909).** Let $f \ge 0$ be product-measurable (sigma-finite factors). Then $y \mapsto \int f^{y} \, dm$ and $x \mapsto \int f_{x} \, dm$ are measurable, and
>
> $$\iint f \, d(m \times m) \ =\ \int \! \Bigl( \int f(x,y) \, dm(x) \Bigr) dm(y) \ =\ \int \! \Bigl( \int f(x,y) \, dm(y) \Bigr) dm(x),$$
>
> all three together, $\infty$ included.

*Proof.* The four-stage reel. *Rectangles*: for $f = \mathbf{1}_{A \times B}$ all three read $m(A) m(B)$ by inspection. *Tribe*: the class of sets whose indicators satisfy the display contains the rectangles and is a monotone class closed under the algebra's operations — the beam (Remark 7.6) carries it to $\mathcal{M} \otimes \mathcal{M}$; sigma-finite frames guard the complementation step (the guided skeleton). *Staircases*: linearity (Chapter 5's discharged additivity, on the plane and the line alike) extends the display to simple functions. *Climb*: the staircase theorem writes $f$ as an increasing simple limit; monotone convergence (Chapter 5) passes the limit through all three integrals at once — the inner integrals climb by MCT on each section, and their integrals climb by MCT again. Rectangles, tribe, staircases, climb. ∎

> **Theorem 7.8 (Fubini, 1907).** Let $f$ be product-measurable with $\iint \lvert f \rvert \, d(m \times m) < \infty$. Then for almost every $y$ the section $f^{y}$ is integrable (and dually), the a.e.- defined iterated integrals exist, and both equal $\iint f \, d(m \times m)$.

*Proof.* Tonelli on $\lvert f \rvert$ prices $\int \bigl( \int \lvert f^{y} \rvert \bigr) dm(y) < \infty$, so the inner integral is finite for a.e. $y$ (Chapter 4's little lemma, I.6, in its finite-a.e. form): bad slices are null, amnestied. Split $f = f^{+} - f^{-}$; Tonelli prices each part's display; subtract — lawful, both totals finite by the hypothesis — section by section on the good slices and integral by integral overall (linearity). ∎

> **Remark 7.9 (The standard operating procedure — canonized).** To swap: if $f \ge 0$, swap (Tonelli). Else compute $\iint \lvert f \rvert$ by either itinerary (Tonelli again — the check itself is swappable); if finite, swap (Fubini); if infinite, do not — you stand at the crime scene. Chapter 5's small promise, discharged; the constitution is Season One's series doctrine (absolute licenses rearrangement) in planar dress.

#### 7.4 The Crime Scene and the Fine Print

> **Proposition 7.10 (The staircase and its shadows).** On $[0,\infty)^2$ let
>
> $$f \ =\ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \Bigl( \mathbf{1}_{[k, k+1) \times [k, k+1)} \; - \; \mathbf{1}_{[k+1, k+2) \times [k, k+1)} \Bigr).$$
>
> Then both iterated integrals exist and
>
> $$\int \! \Bigl( \int f \, dm(y) \Bigr) dm(x) \ =\ 1, \qquad \int \! \Bigl( \int f \, dm(x) \Bigr) dm(y) \ =\ 0,$$
>
> while $\iint \lvert f \rvert = \infty$: the integrability check fails, and no license was issued.

*Proof.* Columns (fix $x \in [j, j+1)$, integrate $dm(y)$): for $j = 0$ the column meets only the $k{=}0$ positive block: inner integral $1$. For $j \ge 1$: the positive block $k = j$ contributes $+1$ on $y \in [j, j+1)$ and the shadow with $k+1 = j$, i.e. $k = j - 1$, contributes $-1$ on $y \in [j-1, j)$: inner integral $0$. Outer: $\int = 1 \cdot 1 = 1$. Rows (fix $y \in [k, k+1)$, integrate $dm(x)$): the storey's positive block on $x \in [k, k+1)$ and its own shadow on $x \in [k+1, k+2)$: inner integral $0$, every $k \ge 0$ — shadows are cast sideways, so no storey lacks one. Outer: $0$. Absolute mass: each of infinitely many blocks carries $1$: $\iint \lvert f \rvert = \infty$ (Tonelli's own count, either order). Diagnosis: the two itineraries are two orderings of the conditionally convergent block-series $1 - 1 + 1 - 1 + \cdots$-flavoured mass; Volume One's rearrangement theorem, staged on the quarter-plane. Solved in full as Problem II.2, block by block. ∎

> **Remark 7.11 (Sigma-finiteness's witness).** Pair $([0,1], m)$ with $([0,1], \#)$ — counting measure, not sigma-finite — and take $f = \mathbf{1}_{\Delta}$, the diagonal's indicator. Then $\int \bigl( \int f \, d\#(y) \bigr) dm(x) = \int 1 \, dm = 1$ (each $x$-section is one point, counted once), while $\int \bigl( \int f \, dm(x) \bigr) d\#(y) = \int 0 \, d\# = 0$ (each $y$-section is one point, length nought). Nonnegative, measurable in the appropriate joint sense, disagreeing: the sigma-finite clause in Theorems 7.7–7.8 is real. (Three lines, as promised; the measurability fine print of the diagonal in the product tribe is the Notes' small-print reference.)

#### 7.5 The Layer Cake

> **Theorem 7.12 (The layer-cake representation).** For measurable $f \ge 0$ on sigma-finite ground $E$:
>
> $$\int_{E} f \, dm \ =\ \int_{0}^{\infty} m\{ x \in E : f(x) > t \} \, dm(t).$$

*Proof.* Tonelli's somersault on the subgraph indicator $\mathbf{1}_{S}$, $S = \{ (x, t) : 0 \le t < f(x) \}$ (product-measurable: $S = \bigcup_{q \in \Q^{+}} \{f > q\} \times [0, q)$-flavoured assembly, Problem II.4). Heights first: $\int_0^\infty \mathbf{1}_S(x, t) \, dm(t) = f(x)$; then ground: the left side. Ground first: $\int_E \mathbf{1}_S(x, t) \, dm(x) = m\{f > t\}$; then heights: the right side. Tonelli licenses the equality unconditionally. — The finale's uniform: expectation equals the integral of tail probabilities. ∎

#### 7.8 Solutions

**Tier I (terse).** **I.3**'s middle: $\int_0^1\!\int_0^1 (x + y) = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12$ by staircase symmetry, either order. **I.6**: $\int_0^1 (1 - t) \, dt$ computed by the identity's own layer cake — the season eating its own cooking. **I.8**: the tent on $[0, 2]$, peak one at $x=1$: $\min(x, 2-x)^{+}$.

**II.2 (solution in full).** As Proposition 7.10, expanded: the column table for $j = 0, 1, 2$ and the general row; the absolute count $\sum_k (1 + 1) = \infty$; and the diagnosis displayed as a rearrangement: enumerate the blocks column-first and the partial sums visit $1$ eternally; row-first and they visit $0$ eternally — two orderings of $\pm 1$ masses, Volume One, Chapter 4's theorem quoted with its chapter number.

**II.6 (solution in full).** *Measurability.* Take $\tilde f$ Borel with $\tilde f = f$ a.e. (Chapter 2, Theorem 2.17 — an $F_\sigma$-built version); then $(x,y) \mapsto \tilde f(x-y)$ is Borel$\circ$continuous: product-Borel-measurable (Chapter 4's safe direction on the plane); $\tilde f(x-y) g(y)$ product-measurable (algebra). The exceptional set $\{ \tilde f(x-y) \ne f(x-y) \}$ is planar-null: its $y$-sections are translates of a line-null set, and Tonelli on its indicator prices it at $\int 0 = 0$. *Pricing.* Tonelli (nonnegative case), inner over $x$ first: $\int f(x-y) \, dm(x) = \lVert f \rVert_1$ for every $y$ (translation invariance), so $\iint = \lVert f \rVert_1 \lVert g \rVert_1 < \infty$. *Existence a.e.* The $x$-sections' finiteness for a.e. $x$ is the little lemma on the finite double integral (via the reversed itinerary — Tonelli again). Signed case: run the above on $\lvert f \rvert, \lvert g \rvert$ for the lid, then Fubini's bookkeeping; $\lVert f * g \rVert_1 \le \lVert f \rVert_1 \lVert g \rVert_1$ by the triangle inequality under the integral. *The algebra of convolution — commutativity, the smoothing folklore — is shelved (Notes); tonight only its existence papers were promised.*

### Chapter 8. Probability Is Measure Theory

*Companion to Episode Eight, the series finale. The episode read Kolmogorov's dictionary item by item (the wonder beat: "you have been using this course your entire career"), made independence a product measure and Episode Seven load-bearing, named Borel–Cantelli (the first lemma being Episode Six's tail-trap, cross-reference stamped), christened Chebyshev and proved the weak law in four sentences, honoured the strong law with a statement and Etemadi's sketch, stated Radon–Nikodym with the devil's staircase as its singular witness (the course's fondest monster retiring as fine print), framed conditional expectation as best guess and projection, set the Kullback–Leibler wink as the course's final star, retraced the arc Hippasus-to-Kolmogorov, audited every account of two seasons aloud (Debt Twelve settled on the spot — the desk executes the payment in Section 8.5 — and one loan gracefully carried beyond, declared), read the seventeen-ring peal one final time, and closed the door. This chapter is the paperwork, and the last. Register notes: **the bell is silent and retires at seventeen**; the full audit is the episode's text, mirrored in the LEDGER; the further-reading essay closes the volume per the plan's final mandate.*

#### Episode Digest

**The argument of the hour.** Probability is this course. Mass-one measure spaces; events are citizens; random variables are measurable functions; distributions are pushforwards; expectation is the integral with all of Chapter 5 attached; almost surely is the amnesty; the convergence zoo transfers with its map. Independence is product measure (factored expectations by the SOP). Borel–Cantelli: finite total risk, finitely many disasters (the tail-trap under its name); independent infinite risk, infinitely many (the complement bound) — a zero-one dichotomy. Chebyshev from the embryo; the weak law by linearity-independence-Chebyshev; the strong law stated with respect. Radon–Nikodym: densities exist exactly under absolute continuity (necessity proved; sufficiency stated with references); the staircase's distribution is singular continuous — mass on the dust, no atoms, no density: the clause's standing witness. Conditional expectation: the R–N dividend; cell averages in the finite case; the projection reading in the seventeenth ring's geometry; the KL divergence as an expected log-derivative — the final star. The audit executes its last payment on the spot: every bounded derivative integrates to the net change of its primitive (Theorem 8.12, dominated convergence presiding) — Debt Twelve's bounded estate recovered as promised. The audit balances; the peal is read; the door closes.
